items.title: The AI Knowledge Society: Mapping Digital Hospitality and Hostility (Panel: traditional / In-Person)
items.location: Wyndham Atlanta Buckhead Hotel and Conference Center * Atlanta, GA · South Atlantic Modern Language Association (SAMLA)

items.fullDescription: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems, in contemporary digital society, have drastically evolved from statistical tools to principal instruments of knowledge production, validation and dissemination. Large language models (LLMs), automated search systems, and predictive algorithms increasingly dictate what society knows, how knowledge is validated, and who is recognized as an expert/authority. This shift demands a rigorous critique from the perspective of the sociology of knowledge to evaluate how power, inequality, and social structures are embedded within these automated epistemic tools. The panel invites contributions that explore this socio-epistemic duality of AI through conflicting dynamics: Societal Hospitality and Structural Hostility. Detailed Description On the surface, consumer-facing AI presents a welcoming, democratic frontier. It offers immediate information access, bridges linguistic barriers, lowers technical entry requirements, and serves as an affordable intellectual assistant. This interface-level hospitality suggests an era of information democratization, flattening historical institutional gatekeeping. Beneath this user-friendly disguise lies an aggressive political economy of knowledge. This infrastructure relies on the extraction of human cognitive labor, the enclosure of the global intellectual commons, and the automated erasure of marginalized ways of knowing. The back end of AI systems enforces a rigid epistemology that encodes historical social biases, presenting them as neutral, objective, mathematical truths. This panel seeks to bring together scholars, theorists, and empirical researchers to map this friction. The panel aims to explore how AI acts simultaneously as an infrastructure of social integration and a vector of epistemic alienation. The panel invites abstracts from scholars at all career stages, encouraging contributions from digital sociology, science and technology studies (STS), critical race studies, media studies, political economy and other interdisciplinary fields. The panel welcomes empirical, theoretical, and methodological papers that address questions including, but not limited to: The Political Economy of Algorithmic Expertise The Erasure of Tacit and Indigenous Knowledge The Deskilling and Alienation of Cognitive Labor Conversational AI as a Trojan Horse Digital Colonialism and Epistemic Homogenization Algorithmic Stratification and Epistemic Class Divides Epistemic Resistance, Subversion, and Counter-Publics The Techno-Religious Frame: AI as the Modern Oracle Reference Benjamin, R. (2019). Race After Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the New Jim Code. Polity. Collins, H. (2024). Why Artificial Intelligence Needs Sociology of Knowledge. Cambridge University Press. Crawford, K. (2021). Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence. Yale University Press. Fricker, M. (2007). Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing. Oxford University Press. Liu, C. (2026). The Sociology of AI as an Emerging Field: Mapping Tensions and Boundaries. Sociology Compass. Zuboff, S. (2019). The Age of Surveillance Capitalism. Public Affairs. Submission Requirements Abstracts: 300-500 words, clearly stating the research problem, theoretical framework, methodology (if empirical), and core argument along with A/V requirements Keywords: 3-5 keywords Biography: A brief biography (100 words) of the author(s)Please send queries, suggestions and scheduling requests to Dr. Amrita Basu Roy Chowdhury (Lady Brabourne College, India) at basuroyamrita1983@gmail.com and/or through the Ballast platform by 31 August 2026. [Please note that all submissions will eventually have to be uploaded through Ballast.]

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers From its inception, cinema has transcended borders through the movement of people, capital, narratives, and visual technology. However, over the past two decades, the term transnational cinema has evolved into one of the most influential and contested frameworks in film studies. Scholars such as Elizabeth Ezra, Terry Rowden, Deborah Shaw, Will Higbee, and Song Hwee Lim have variously expanded, critiqued, and redefined the concept, emphasizing its aesthetic, political, and industrial dimensions and prompting new questions about its theoretical and pedagogical implications. While these approaches have illuminated the circulation of films, filmmakers, and spectators across borders, they have also raised questions about the continuing relevance of the national cinema framework and the analytical boundaries of the transnational itself. This symposium revisits the concept of transnational cinema at a moment when two distinct currents seem bound for collision. On the one hand, global migration, digital media, the global climate catastrophe, geopolitical conflicts, and transregional collaborations have blurred distinctions between the local and the global, as well as the national and the transnational. On the other hand, isolationism, authoritarianism, and protectionism have re-erected physical and ideological borders across the globe. Is the world more or less transnational as a result of these competing impulses? We invite proposals that address theoretical, historical, or pedagogical questions, such as: How can the familiar concept of transnational cinema elucidate emergent and unfamiliar problems in the contemporary landscape? How do we define and teach transnational cinema now? Is transnational cinema best understood as a framework, an approach, a mode of filmmaking, or a category of world cinema? How does transnational cinema intersect with, or diverge from, national, world, and global cinema theories? What are the political, aesthetic, or ethical stakes of emphasizing transnationality in film studies today? We welcome both theoretical interventions and case studies from diverse regions and traditions. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: • Theories and definitions of transnational cinema • Pedagogical approaches to transnational cinema • Feminist, queer, and trans approaches to transnational cinema • Transnational authorship and stardom • Memory, trauma, and postmemory in transnational film • Digital technologies and virtual transnational spaces • Streaming platforms and global distribution • Cinemas of diaspora, exile, and migration • Cross-border activism and solidarity through film • Environmental and ecological transnationalism • Film policy, censorship, and cultural diplomacy • Transnational labor, precarity, and creative economies • International film festivals and global circulation • Archival and historiographical approaches to transnational film • Politics of translation, dubbing, and subtitling • Regional and transregional filmmaking practices • Anti-colonial, postcolonial, and de-colonial aesthetics and narratives • Global Hollywood and transnational co-productions• Transnational spectatorship and global audiences • State, statelessness, and belonging in transnational cinema • Borders, border-crossings, and redefinitions of home • Transnational genres • De-Westernizing film studies Presenters will be invited to submit completed papers for consideration in an edited collection or special issue developed from the symposium. Proposals (250-300 words) and short bios (100 words) should be submitted by June 1st, 2026, using this Google Form: https://forms.gle/R7Jw98KpMEc7BAHo6 For questions, please contact the organizing committee at ahtfilmstudies@utdallas.edu.

items.excerpt: Tentative Title- Beyond the Ocean: Maritime Infrastructure and Hydro-Narratives of Indians under the Raj Concept Note The imperial ships of the British Raj bore millions of Indian migrants across waterways just the way Charon ferried souls across the river Styx to an irreversible fate. items.fullDescription: Tentative Title- Beyond the Ocean: Maritime Infrastructure and Hydro-Narratives of Indians under the Raj Concept Note The imperial ships of the British Raj bore millions of Indian migrants across waterways just the way Charon ferried souls across the river Styx to an irreversible fate. Nonetheless, the Indians transformed the vicious vessels into spaces of radical rebirth and enduring kinship. While the first volume in this series geographically mapped the global representations of Indian migration under the British Empire, Volume 2 moves into a critical interrogation of colonial history through ports, maritime framework, and waterways. Moving away from land-bound histories, this volume initiates an intensive interrogation of colonial history through its maritime infrastructures: ports, dockyards, maritime records, and waterways. This book adopts a hydrocolonial and aqua-centric hermeneutic to explore how subaltern narratives were historically erased from official imperial records, shipping registers, and mainstream historiography. It will examine the ports, vessels, inland rivers, and vast oceans that witnessed the diverse, turbulent flows of Indian populations across the globe. We invite chapter proposals that explore how literary depictions illustrate the ways the British Empire transformed global waterways into networks of imperial power, capital, and radical identity transformation. The psychological and structural undoing of native culture began long before the ship reached the open ocean. In the liminal, high-stress spaces of the colonial dockyards and ports, social hierarchies began to collapse. Diaspora literature, folk traditions, travelogues, and ship logs frequently evoke the immediate and profound breakdown of caste and religious boundaries the moment emigrants set foot on the regimented ports. Sudden intermixing occurred in these crowded transit camps as we witnessed Brahmins consuming food prepared by lower-caste hands, Hindus and Muslims shared sleeping quarters, and sacred visual markers of identity (turbans, sacred threads, prayer beads, religious caps, and tilaks) were stripped or voluntarily discarded to avoid surveillance, standing out, or segregation upon reaching destination ports. Once aboard, the ship itself became a volatile micro-world, sort of floating world suspended between an old life and an uncertain future. Significantly, many post-slavery labour migrations repurposed slave ships to transport new, freer workforce alongside other cargo. Textual representations from this middle passage vividly capture the horrors of overcrowding, disease, and racial prejudice. Yet, the vessel can be read as a site of profound subaltern resilience. Indian migrants forged deep, enduring bonds that acted as vital substitutes for the blood relations left behind, helping them survive the culture shock and grief of displacement. The songs, stories, and archives of this passage are filled with narratives of maritime resistance, shipboard revolts, and haunting tragedies that demand our critical attention. Book II of the Beyond the Ocean series invites proposals that capture the Indian migrant experience from port to port during the British Raj. Echoing Kamau Brathwaite's conceptualization of the tidal experience, we welcome essays that explore the large-scale, long-term dispersion of Indians across the global maritime network, starting from the Gulf nations and the African continent to Southeast Asia, American states, and the archipelagic Caribbean islands. Suggested areas for submission, including, but not limited to: Literary depictions of port architecture, custom houses, dockyards, and the initial dismantling of caste/religious identities. Ship as a total institution, the legacy of repurposed slave ships, and narratives of disease, discipline, and imperial surveillance at sea. Textual and musical representations of shipboard kinship, solidarity, and emotional survival among diverse migrant groups. Songs, oral histories, and literary accounts of maritime mutinies, escapes, sabotage, and shipboard tragedies. How the crossing of the Kala Pani (black waters) fractured and reshaped languages, creating creolized idioms, plantation songs, and hybrid oral traditions. Comparative literary readings of different aquatic journeys- including indentured labourers, penal convicts, Lascar sailors, Kangani System, Maistry System, Sepoys, and Colonial Constabularies, and free passage merchants. Literary representation of Indian ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and other water bodies. Literary representation of ship and its infrastructure. Literary representation of the ocean as repository of forgotten/suppressed history and marginalized culture. Comparative study of the Middle Passage and the Kala Pani crossing or other hydro-crossings and its literary representation. Abstract submission deadline: 31st July 2026 Word limit: 250- 350 words with 4-5 keywords Submissions in a word document along with a brief bio-note to be sent to: shubhankukochar@outlook.com You can find Book I (Beyond the Ocean: Literature, History and the British Empire) via this link https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-981-95-2137-1. Note: As Book I was published by Springer, the editors have submitted the proposal for Book II to Springer as well, aiming to establish this as a long-running series. Editors: Dr. Shubhanku Kochar (Associate Professor, University School of Humanities and Social Sciences at Guru Gobind Singh Indraprastha University, Delhi) Dr. Shehnaz Kabir (Research and Development Officer, Loreto College, Kolkata)

items.fullDescription: The Centre for Comparative Modernities (CCM) invites proposals for thirty-minute papers for their 2026/27 Autumn Workshop series. Proposals are welcome from doctoral and Early Career Researchers from across all disciplines. The seminar series offers the opportunity to present research (both ongoing and completed) and to receive informal feedback from peers. As a centre CCM aims to foster an interdisciplinary perspective that moves beyond the Western-centric paradigm of modernity and to challenge conventional understandings of how the world has changed over time. Papers focused on international and comparative approaches are particularly welcome. Topics may include but are not limited to: · Localising Modernity · Modernity and Westernisation · Transnational modernities · East Asian modernities · Philosophical perspectives on modernities · Technological Modernities · Modernity and Gender · Modernity and Cultural Transitions · Modernity and Orientalism Please submit a title and abstract of no more than 200 words along with a short biography (max. 100 words) to ccm@durham.ac.uk by 31 August 2026. All sessions will be held online. You can find out more about the centre's activities and opportunities on X (Twitter) @ccmdurham or on our website: https://www.durham.ac.uk/research/institutes-and-centres/centre-for-comparative-modernities/

items.fullDescription: Abstract: This panel reexamines life writing in the age of Generative AI, asking who controls the conditions under which individuals narrate their own lives. Submissions reflecting on how AI corporations and Generative AI models are reshaping life writing practices across textual, digital, and visual formats, or on the consequences of such practices for authorship, equity, and cultural power, are especially welcome. Full CFP: Generative AI has fundamentally changed how we think, articulate, and write. However, access to AI is not equitable, and its outputs frequently fail to account for diverse lived experiences and reflect biases. The corporations developing AI models are agents actively reshaping how we perceive, think, interpret, and articulate our identities and experiences. This panel examines what that means for Life Writing - defined broadly to include textual, digital, and visual formats - where individuals reflect, narrativize, and present their lived experiences in public-facing contexts. Submissions engaging the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," are especially welcome. The panel welcomes submissions that explore (but are not limited to): a) Questions of authorship for AI-assisted/AI-mediated life writings b) The aesthetics and formal transformations in the practice of Life Writing in the age of Generative AI c) Life Writings produced by or attributed to Generative AI models d) The 'Author' Persona in AI-generated/AI-mediated Life Writing e) Autoethnographic explorations of writing life with AI f) Reader/Audience response to AI-mediated/AI-generated life writings g) Questions of ethics, trust, and safety, when narrating life with AI h) Impacts of AI-mediated life writing on individuals from vulnerable and marginalized communities, diverse gender identities, racial, and cultural communities i) "Permanent Memory" of AI models and archival of individual identities j) Translation, multilingualism, and cultural limitations of Generative AI in supporting Life Writing activities Note: > Please submit your proposals only via the link: https://pamla.ballastacademic. com/Home/S/20174 > Extended Deadline to submit proposals is June 30, 2026 ; early submissions are encouraged. > The 2026 PAMLA Conference is entirely in person , in Seattle, WA, with no provision for virtual or hybrid presentations . > Please check the PAMLA website for dates and additional information

items.fullDescription: "Rhetorical Theory" (Standing Session) Seattle, WA, Nov. 20-23 Chair: Dr. Ryan Leack (USC) Email: leack@usc.edu Abstract This panel will explore recent movements in rhetorical theory writ large, either in connection with or apart from composition theory and practice. Special attention will be given to proposals that engage with the conference's theme. Description In addition to expanding rhetoric's disciplinary relations, this panel hopes to push rhetoric beyond persuasion-beyond rhetoric as purposeful action toward some given end, but also as reception, listening, responsivity, relationality, resonance, presence, aurality, and the like. In this way, the panel hopes to push rhetoric's boundaries and find kinship in new frontiers beyond its disciplinary and historically sanctioned borders. This panel invites papers which explore rhetorical theory in general, but prefers papers which relate rhetoric, specifically or generally, to the below topics: o Rhetorical listening o Orality and/vs. aurality o Rhetorical new materialisms o Sound studies o Sonic rhetoric o New/materialisms o Quantum/physics o Agential realism o Posthumanism o Empiricism o Object-oriented rhetoric o Object-oriented ontology o Affect theory Abstract Length : 150-200 words Abstract Deadline : May 25, 2026 Please Submit Abstract through PAMLA website : https://pamla.ballastacademic.com/Home/S/19615

items.fullDescription: Italian Teaching Symposium 2026 - II edition "Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching" September 25-26, 2026 St. Jerome's University (University of Waterloo) & online Inspired by the theme chosen for the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, "Lingua geniale: ideare, progettare, creare con l'italiano", we are pleased to announce the second edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium, once again endorsed by the Canadian Association for Italian Studies (CAIS). Building on the success of its inaugural 2025 edition, which welcomed more than fifty participants - including presenters, chairs, and attendees from both academia and cultural institutions - this year's symposium will take place on September 25-26, 2026, at St. Jerome's University, federated with the University of Waterloo (Ontario, Canada). While primarily designed as an in-person event, limited opportunities for remote participation may be available. The second edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium, Creative Pathways in Italian Language and Culture Teaching, aims to bring together scholars, researchers, language educators, teacher trainers, graduate students, and practitioners interested in exploring three interconnected dimensions of Italian language education: imagine, design, and create. As Marcel Danesi (2025) observes, "the study of creativity crosses all disciplinary boundaries", making creativity a particularly productive lens through which to examine the teaching and learning of Italian language and culture. This resonates well with the theme of the XXVI Week of the Italian Language in the World, inspired by the newly established Directorate General for Growth and Export Promotion of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which highlights the creative potential of Italian as a language capable of fostering ideas, innovation, and intercultural dialogue. In this sense, teaching Italian extends beyond the transmission of grammar and pronunciation to encompass cultural mediation, collaboration, and engagement with diverse forms of expression. In this context, we invite proposals that reflect on how this perspective inspires - or challenges - instructors to adopt creative and unconventional approaches to course design, including content, activities, teaching methods, and assessment. In addition to traditional paper presentations, the 2026 edition of the Italian Teaching Symposium will introduce a new hands-on session format designed to foster practical exchange, experimentation, and collaborative learning. These interactive sessions will give participants the opportunity to showcase classroom activities, digital tools and apps, pedagogical resources, multimodal projects, creative assignments, community-engaged initiatives, assessment tools, or other innovative practices implemented in Italian language and culture courses. This format is intended to encourage active engagement and discussion, allowing attendees to learn directly from colleagues' experiences and to leave the symposium with practical ideas and materials that can be adapted to their own teaching contexts. Suggested?topics:?? Imagine? Exploring how Italian language and culture can be reimagined as spaces for creativity, identity formation, intercultural dialogue, and social engagement -new perspectives on Italian language, culture, and identity? -intercultural competence and global citizenship through Italian studies? -new imaginaries of Italy,?Italianness, and Italian-speaking communities? -heritage learners, multilingualism, and transnational Italian identities -the future of Italian studies and language programs in changing educational landscapes -reimagining the role of Italian language education in contemporary society? ? Design? Examining the pedagogical, technological, and curricular frameworks that shape innovative Italian language education -curriculum development and innovative pedagogical models? -project-based learning in Italian language education? -multilingual and intercultural learning environments? -educational technologies, AI, and digital course design? -assessment design and innovative evaluation practices -Italian for specific purposes (LSP) and professional communication? -international collaborations and virtual exchange projects? ? Create? Investigating creative practices, cultural production, and multimodal forms of expression in Italian language and culture teaching. -creative writing and storytelling in Italian language?pedagogy? -language learning through music, performance, theatre, cinema,?and?visual arts?? -literature in the Italian classroom?as a tool for language acquisition and cultural?awareness? -student-generated content and multimodal?literacy? -digital creativity and media production -community-engaged learning, public humanities projects, digital creativity, and collaborations beyond the classroom? ? Submission Guidelines? We invite proposals for individual papers (15 minutes), thematic panels (90 minutes), and hands-on workshops (approximately 30 minutes) designed to engage participants in innovative pedagogical practices, classroom activities, digital tools and apps, teaching resources, and creative approaches to Italian language and culture education.? Submissions should include the presentation title, author name(s) and affiliation(s), an abstract in English or Italian of no more than 300 words, and a contact e-mail address. Proposals should be submitted via this form by July 25 , 2026. Notification of acceptance will be sent by July 24, 2026. Questions may be addressed to the symposium organizers, Gianmarco Bocchi (gbocchi@uwaterloo.ca) and Alessia Ursella (aursella@uoguelph.ca).?

items.fullDescription: Date: October 10-11, 2026 Location: SMU Main Campus, Dallas, TX Theme: Movement & Borderlands Abstract Submission Deadline: August 28, 2026 Keynotes: Dr. Tim Bowman & Dr. Elda María Román Graduate students of Southern Methodist University's Departments of English, History, and Anthropology, in collaboration with the Moody School of Advanced Studies, Dedman College Interdisciplinary Institute, and the department of English, have collaborated to hold the third annual Engaging Research Across the Humanities (ERAH) Conference at SMU from October 10-October 11, 2026. ERAH 2026 will prioritize the development of interdisciplinary connections and aims to foster a supportive environment for both graduate students and advanced undergraduates engaged in strong research. There will be special emphasis placed on creating opportunities for participants with limited or no prior conference experience. The theme for ERAH 2026 is Movement & Borderlands. If you have any questions, please email arundhatig@smu.edu. Borders simultaneously construct and limit meaning. By demarcating entities, we hold the power to define space and identity. In the same manner, those entities are restricted to oppositional definitions. What does it mean to occupy borderlands, to move across them and through them? How is the deconstruction of borders, or reconceptualization of definitional demarcation, itself an act of meaning-making that exists without opposition? How do borderlands complicate cultural conceptions rooted in duality? How does movement across and through borderlands produce opportunity for new forms of meaning-making not rooted in hard lines and limitations? This year's theme asks us to think critically about the roles of both movement and borderlands in our respective disciplines by considering these questions and others. We invite you to consider the roles of both movement and borderlands within the works you study-be it literary works, historical archives, etc.-as well as how pervasive disciplinary paradigms shape the ways in which you approach your scholarship. Possible topics may include but are not limited to: Migration, mobility, and displacement Citizenship and belonging Racial, ethnic, national, religious identity Borders as constructs Frontiers Artistic and embodied movement Indigenous perspectives on imposed borders Nationalism and borderlands Environmental and ecological borders Linguistic borders Tourism and global circulation We invite abstracts of 200-250 words for both individual presentations and fully-constructed panels (3-4 speakers). Papers in STEM fields that clearly articulate relevance to the theme are welcome. Full-panel proposals will be given priority. Panel proposals must include a 200-250 word proposal for the panel in addition to abstracts for each individual participant. A select number of travel grants will be awarded on a competitive basis for those traveling more than 100 miles. To qualify for a travel grant, you must submit your application by August 14, 2026. Further details will be included in your registration sign-up. Please submit abstracts via the following google form link: https://tinyurl.com/2026ERAH

items.title: Déplacements dans les réseaux transcoloniaux : l'Asie, l’Afrique et l’Europe reliés
items.excerpt: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. items.fullDescription: Pendant la période de l'Indochine française, les premiers vietnamiens sont acheminés en Nouvelle-Calédonie en tant que travailleurs sous-contrat dans les mines de nickel. Cette période marque en parallèle la rébellion très présente des autochtones de l'île - les Kanak - face à la dépossession territoriale des colons français. Le refus de participer à l'industrie minière d'un groupe favorise l'expatriation de l'autre sur l'archipel en pleine ère de la colonisation française dans plusieurs colonies. Le roi tonkinois Ham Nghi, à l'âge de 18 ans, a été placé en exil en Algérie après des années de mouvements de résistance contre la puissance coloniale française. Son expulsion fait écho à celle de la Reine malgache Ranavalona III, qui a eu lieu après l'annexion de Madagascar par la France en 1896. L'ensemble de l'empire français, étendu de l'Indochine à l'Afrique insulaire, est sujet à la déportation dans la plus grande colonie de peuplement. Ce réseau de déportation des colonies liées met en avant la question des outils de domination employés par le système colonial. Malgré les différentes populations colonisées, la stratégie de domination s'applique d'une certaine façon. **** Dans le cadre académique au sein des études francophones et françaises, nous voyons souvent des pistes de spécialisation distinctes, telles que les études européennes, les études caribéennes, et les études postcoloniales francophones. Les cours d'histoire et de littérature offrent également des réflexions particulières selon une région spécifique ainsi qu'une époque donnée. L'objectif de former les futurs chercheurs dans des domaines précis, faute d'études approfondies sur les caractéristiques transcontinentales, risque de faire oublier qu'au coeur de l'histoire de l'un est tissée celle de l'autre. Cette imbrication transnationale et transcommunautaire, inévitable soit-elle, est due à la fois aux déplacements migratoires, à l'exil d'après-guerre, et à la mobilisation de la force de travail par le système capitaliste et colonial. Lorsque l'on met en évidence ce lien intrinsèque entre des événements, on fait émerger un réseau transcolonial qui lie l'Afrique, l'Asie, et/ou l'Europe. Ce réseau nous oblige à réfléchir à l'interconnexion de l'un à l'autre, d'une communauté spécifique à une autre soi-disant éloignée. Dans le contexte du monde d'aujourd'hui, une telle conscience de l'interconnexion des histoires coloniales peut susciter des réflexions : Peut-on vraiment ignorer le combat de l'autre ? Quels seront les enjeux ? Communications à envoyer soit en anglais, soit en français.

items.fullDescription: The sea and marine life are often considered as pillars of cultural heritage, identity, and collective memories in Portugal (Lourenço 2001; Lourenço 2014). From the historical milestones of the sixteenth century transoceanic navigation (Cortesão 1978) to literary production (Avelar 2024), the ocean has shaped the national imagination of Portugal (Tomás 2013). As Antonio Barreto writes: "Heritage is a human creation and the results from history and culture. But there are natural realities that are transformed, through history, culture, and technology into heritage. Such is the case of the sea for the Portuguese" (2019: 15). As a form of heritage, this connection extends to gastronomy and, in a particularly profound way, to the musical sphere (Simões 2013: 45-62; Sardo 2013: 44-64). From fado, with its narratives of longing and loss, to the songs that gave rhythm to the the fishermen's daily work, the Portuguese musical repertoire has functioned as a living archive of human interaction with the environment. However, there is nothing natural or essentialist about this Portuguese relationship with the sea, for it is an imaginary that has been constructed and continously negotiated across historical periods, which also bears the imprint of colonialism (João 2015: 119-147; El-Shawan Castelo-Branco et al 2003: 73-142). More dramatically, the transformations driven by climate change and unsustainable industrial fishing in the twenty-first century threaten not only biodiversity (Ramos-Pereira 2004: 26-43), but also the cultural practices linked to it - a topic that still requires greater attention in schoarly research. In any case, beyond its material and economic dimensions, the sea in Portugal remains a space of imagination and transformation. As evoked in the songs of José Afonso, the sea is not just a site of identity and homecoming, but also a place of alterity and utopia. By singing of the sea, we evoke the possibility of a new era, in which culture and nature meet once again in a shared project of humanity - a vision that also resonates with the notion of the Blue Humanities (Mentz 2023; Oppermann 2019: 443-461). This call seeks to explore the intersection between what we have inherited and what we must protect. Therefore, we invite researchers, artists, and cultural practitioners to reflect on how these environmental changes reshape the meaning of the arts and their role as vehicles of identity and resistance. Papers are welcome on the following topics, amongst others: The sea as a cultural construct in Portuguese music and the arts; Music, critique, and resistance to climate crises in Portugal; Intersections between literature, music, and environmental heritage; Representations of the sea and music in literature and written culture; Music, sound, identity, and the politics of ocean memory; Collective memory, local identities, and soundscapes; The sea in film, the media, and popular culture; Folklore, folk groups, and the preservation of intangible cultural heritage; Coloniality and decoloniality of contemporary maritime identity; Transcultural and postcolonial perspectives on the maritime imaginary; Blue Humanities and music as an environmental archive; Resistance, utopia, and sound activism in the face of climate change; Tourism and heritage preservation of coastal musical cultures; Technology, marine sciences, and music; Ocean ethics, music, and maritime imaginaries; Phenomenology, aesthetics, listening, and maritime experience. Submission Guidelines Proposals should be sent to the email: cecc.fch@ucp.pt, and include paper title, A 300-word abstract in Portuguese or in English should be submitted for a 20-minute presentation, including a provisional title, a brief biographical note (max. 150 words) and contact details. Contributions may be in Portuguese or English. items.fullDescription: Abstract : This roundtable explores contemporary directions in life writing, biography, and memoir, with a particular interest in how we narrate the self amidst evolving issues of identity, culture, and power. We welcome both traditional scholarly essays and creative nonfiction/memoir submissions accompanied by a brief meta-analysis. Potential topics include, but are not limited to, autoethnography, digital self-representation, intersectional approaches to life writing, and the emerging impacts of technological shifts-such as generative AI-on authorship and equity. Desctription : How do we articulate, preserve, and present our lived experiences in an era marked by rapid cultural and technological change? Aligning with the conference theme, "Our Ruling Classes: Culture, Power and Conflict," this roundtable invites participants to investigate the shifting landscape of life writing across textual, digital, and visual formats. To foster a vibrant, multi-voiced dialogue, we encourage submissions from a wide range of perspectives, including traditional literary criticism, biographical studies, and creative pieces that feature a reflective or meta-analytical component. Presenters will deliver brief, 10-to-12-minute talks to maximize time for collective discussion. items.fullDescription: Building Bridges: Preparing for Global Business (39th Annual IATEFL BESIG Conference) When : Friday, November 20, 2026 (13.00 CET / 12.00 UK time) - Sunday, November 22, 2026 (14.00 CET / 13.00 UK time) Venue : Hotel Flemings Wien Stadthalle in Vienna, Austria. Call for Proposals Business English education sits at the intersection of education, professional communication, and global social change. In a world shaped by geopolitical tensions, economic inequalities, technological disruption, and cultural polarization, communication across cultural contexts is both more necessary and more complex than ever. Business English therefore involves more than teaching linguistic skills for the workplace; it also prepares learners to deal with cultural diversity, power structures, and ethical decision-making in international professional contexts. Effective professional communication today requires not only exchanging information but also negotiating meaning, building trust, and collaborating across cultures and perspectives. Business English courses support university students, vocational learners, and professionals in developing communicative competence, intercultural awareness, and confidence in multilingual workplaces. In many contexts, this work involves collaboration with corporate partners and engagement with current workplace practices, while also encouraging critical reflection on whose voices are heard in professional communication. The role of the business English educator is therefore to help learners bridge multiple gaps: between education and professional practice, between various cultures, and between local experiences and global systems. In a fragmented and rapidly changing world, business English education can help create spaces for inclusive, responsible, and effective professional communication. This year's conference invites contributions that explore how business English education can respond to these challenges and build the bridges needed for meaningful intercultural understanding. We particularly welcome contributions that combine practical experience, innovative teaching approaches, and reflective insights from educational and professional contexts. ----------------- Thank you for your interest in submitting a speaker proposal for the 39th IATEFL BESIG Conference. Only members of IATEFL BESIG can present at the conference. You may submit a proposal if you are not a member; however, if your proposal is accepted, you will be required to join IATEFL BESIG in order to be included in the programme. The call for proposals is open until 30 June 2026 at 16:00 (UK time). Click here for more information: https://www.iateflbesig.org/events/annual-conference

items.title: Artificial/Ancestral: Black Theatre and the Question of AI
items.excerpt: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these tec...
items.fullDescription: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these technologies have arrived without history, entering an empty landscape awaiting innovation. Yet Black theatre has long grappled with questions of representation, embodiment, archives, intellectual inheritance, collective memory, labor, and futurity. Rather than asking simply what AI can do for Black theatre, this issue invites contributors to consider what Black theatre reveals about AI itself: its assumptions, limitations, aspirations, and consequences. Volume 4.2 of the Black Theatre Review seeks essays, interviews, case studies, pedagogical interventions, archival investigations, artist statements, and process reflections that place Black theatre and performance studies in critical conversation with artificial intelligence and related technologies. We are particularly interested in work that moves beyond questions of adoption, utility, or rejection toward deeper examinations of power, ethics, governance, memory, embodiment, and knowledge production. We welcome contributions from scholars, artists, archivists, educators, practitioners, dramaturgs, designers, and cultural workers whose engagement with these questions emerges from both theory and practice. The issue is organized around five interrelated areas of inquiry. These themes are offered not as rigid categories, but as points of departure for further investigation. Taken together, these areas encourage contributors to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a site through which questions of labor, memory, embodiment, governance, spirituality, and future-making can be reconsidered. AI, Labor and Extraction: The beneficiaries of AI systems, whose labor makes them possible and required forms of accountability when Black creative work becomes data. Possible points of investigation may include: The labor of artists whose knowledge underlies any AI-readable record and what ethical stewardship of that labor requires. Generative AI in dramaturgy, script analysis, and design workflows, and models of artist-led intentional integration. Archives, Memory, and Black Theatre Histories: How do AI systems shape, distort, recover, or fail to capture Black theatrical histories and modes of remembering? Possible points of investigation may include: Digitization and AI-training projects involving Black theatre collections and their assumptions about what counts as trainable data. AI-assisted archival misreadings, flattening, erasure, and historical distortion. Embodiment, Liveness, and Performance: What happens when embodied, communal, and improvisational performance practices encounter technologies built on prediction, simulation, and abstraction? Possible points of investigation may include: Case studies of AI in the classroom, rehearsal hall, or production process. The complementary offerings of embodied, ensemble-based theatre training to university-wide AI adoption. Relatedly, how do such offerings get recognized, funded, or institutionally protected? Ancestral Intelligence, Spiritual Knowledge, and Black Futures: Understanding AI as a knowledge system entering into conversation with much older Black diasporic traditions of intelligence, memory, and futurity Possible points of investigation may include: AI as ancestral intelligence, or Black diasporic traditions of pattern recognition, forecasting, memory, and knowledge transmission. How do Black diasporic understandings of knowledge, memory, inheritance, ritual, and collective survival shape the technological futures we imagine? Refusal, Governance, and Alternative Technological Practices: Forms of resistance, opacity, governance, and the possibilities of misuse Possible points of investigation may include: How Black artists are bending, breaking, or refusing AI against its intended use. Teaching against technological inevitability. Photograph, Visual Media, and Digital Project Documentation tBTR welcomes photographic, visual media, and digital project documentation that illuminates the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We encourage submissions featuring productions, rehearsals, classroom projects, design processes, digital or hybrid performances, archival initiatives, community-based projects, and artistic experiments that engage the themes of this issue. Submissions may include production photography, design renderings, screenshots, interface documentation, archival images, process documentation, and other visual materials that help narrate how artists, scholars, educators, and institutions are critically engaging AI and related technologies. All submissions must include the project or production title, names and roles of key collaborators, location, creator and/or photographer credit, date, and a 2-3 sentence description explaining the work's relationship to the issue's focus on labor, archives, embodiment, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, ancestral knowledge, refusal, governance, or Black futures. Contributors are responsible for securing all necessary permissions and reproduction rights prior to submission. Please contact the managing editor for additional information. Book Reviews, Performance Reviews, and Notes from the Field, and Multimedia Works In addition to scholarly articles, tBTR seeks book reviews, performance reviews, multimedia works, illustrative case studies, and notes from the field that engage the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We are particularly interested in contributions that document pedagogical experimentation, archival initiatives, institution-building efforts, production processes, dramaturgical and design practices, community engagement, and artist-led technological interventions. We also welcome reflections on the ethical, political, and aesthetic questions surrounding AI, including issues of labor, extraction, memory, embodiment, governance, ancestral intelligence, resistance, and alternative technological futures. Submission Guidelines The last date for submissions is September 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT. Please refer to the tBTR website for specific article section guidelines. Manuscripts must be submitted in Microsoft Word using standard formatting (1-inch margins, double-spaced, single-column layout, and 12-point Times New Roman font). Please include an abstract and a 150-word author biography with your submission. All submissions must include footnotes and a bibliography and must fully comply with The Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), using the notes and bibliography system. Please do not use the author-date citation system or another style guide. Please upload your complete manuscript through the journal's online submission portal via the website. Early submissions will receive preference in the review and publication process.

items.fullDescription: The Société Rencesvals, Pan-American Branch, invites proposals from scholars whose research examines Romance-language epics as sites of social discourse. Far from being merely “songs of deeds,” these texts were critical commentaries on contemporary ideologies. They thus speak profoundly to processes of self-conceptualization in far-ranging topics including –but not limited to– regional/national identity, faith, gender, and race. We are interested in the examination of how Romance-language epics use discourse to construct value systems that contribute to conceptions of the self, situating this literature in the larger study of the production of ideologies in the Middle Ages.

items.excerpt: India's civilizational ethos is deeply rooted in its multilingual and multicultural fabric, where translation has enabled the circulation of ideas, texts, and knowledge across regions and traditions. Etymologically understood as "carrying across," translation in the 21st century extends beyond linguistic transfer to become a critical and interpretive prac...
items.fullDescription: India's civilizational ethos is deeply rooted in its multilingual and multicultural fabric, where translation has enabled the circulation of ideas, texts, and knowledge across regions and traditions. Etymologically understood as "carrying across," translation in the 21st century extends beyond linguistic transfer to become a critical and interpretive practice. A. K. Ramanujan, in his writings, draws attention to translation's context-sensitive nature, while G. N. Devy highlights the complex linguistic and cultural histories within which translation operates in India. Seen in this light, translation involves negotiation, re-articulation, and the making of new meanings within specific cultural settings. Practices such as transcreation, adaptation, and interpretation highlight the creative potential of translation. At the same time, the increasing use of machine translation and AI-based tools has introduced another dimension, making translation faster and more accessible, while also raising questions about accuracy and interpretation. In view of these varied contexts, practices, and concerns, this seminar aims to provide a platform for students, teachers, and researchers to reflect on the evolving role of translation in contemporary India across literary, academic, and everyday contexts. It seeks to bring together diverse perspectives on both the challenges and possibilities of translating Indian languages in the present day. Submissions are invited on the following themes: Translation in the classroom: pedagogy and practice Translation and cultural contexts: negotiation and interpretation Translating literary and non-literary texts Translation and cultural pluralism Translation across media: cinema, OTT, and digital platforms AI in translation: possibilities and challenges Translation, representation, and questions of voice Adaptation, transcreation, and rewriting Ethics and responsibilities in translation Emerging trends and research in translation studies The seminar is being held in Hybrid Mode. Register here: https://forms.gle/zYjXGehoDCu85UNm7

items.fullDescription: Plastic / Plasticity Literature and Culture and the Material of a (Bygone?) Era Plastic is a defining material of our era. Its properties—plasticity, durability, the ability to imitate any shape, its toxicity, and indecomposability—are also properties of contemporary culture and literature. The proposed thematic issue begins with the premise that plastic can be read simultaneously as a historical substance and as a "theory machine"—a tool for understanding cultural texts and the experience of contemporary times. "My approach, in this paper, is one of thinking with plastic through its metaphoricity and materiality, its relationality and gestationality; in short, a material mediality.” [R. Gosh]

items.fullDescription: The Department of English-Language Literatures and Cultures and the Institute of Literary Studies at UWM are pleased to invite you to an international interdisciplinary conference on H.G. Wells and Modernity: Texts, Contexts, (Re)visions 22nd-24th Oct. 2026 University of Warmia and Mazury in Olsztyn, Poland Celebrating H.G. Wells's 160th/80th anniversaries of birth and death (1866-1946), this conference invites scholars from across literary studies, linguistics, film studies, political theory, sociology, history, philosophy, and other disciplines to examine modernity's (con)texts through Wells, his contemporaries, and his followers. We aim to consider how their visions reshape understandings of the evolution and devolution of the human, humanity, and society. In many of his literary and non-literary texts, Wells diagnosed the shortcomings of class structures and anticipated modernity's ills, imaginatively prefiguring many current ways of conceptualising the human in relation to the nonhuman. He started as one of the most prolific and versatile short story writers of the late nineteenth century, and he ended as one of the most celebrated sociological and political writers of the first half of the twentieth century. His views, shaped by a complex and troubled faith in science and reason, helped crystallize the formulation of pivotal documents such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. He died disillusioned that the new world which he had envisioned had not arrived, or worse, frustrated to see his darkest predictions materialise. Undermined and still overlooked as a literary figure by the modernists, who could not see eye to eye with him despite initial friendships, who is H.G. Wells for posterity, that is, our times? In asking this question, we recognize that Wells's legacy cannot be confined to Anglophone literary history alone, and it still speaks urgently to contemporary crises of technology, social fragmentation and political imagination. We especially welcome approaches that could help us position Wells and other modernity/modernist writers within transnational literary networks and explore their influence on and dialogue with world literatures. These topics and others are most welcome, among the proposed conference focus points related to H.G. Wells: ? Author's sources: from antiquity to Jonathan Swift, Charles Dickens, Edgar Allan Poe, and others. ? Modernity and the new ways of writing: short story, scientific romance, science fiction. ? Modern aesthetics and the fictional world: literary and linguistic patterns. Representations of the human and humanity: ecocritical, cognitive, postcolonial, and other postmodern and post-postmodern re-readings. ? Wells and international fantastic and science fiction: comparative perspectives across French (Jules Verne), German, and other contexts. ? Wells's legacy in Polish literature: Stanis?aw Lem and others. ? Dialogues and contentions with Joseph Conrad, E.M. Forster, Virginia Woolf, and Henry James. ? Literary and linguistic depictions of science, catastrophe, and war. ? Shifting cultural concepts: evolution and devolution, tensions of power, ambiguities of colonial appropriation. ? Intermedia reinterpretations: film, graphic novels, games, and other media. ? Wells in translation. ? Political thought and the concept of world state. ? Models of femininity and social change. ? Wells and his engagement with history and the future. ? Utopias and dystopias of Wells and other writers. items.fullDescription: Congreso Estética(s) del Horror: Filosofía, Cine y Literatura. Invitación a envío de propuestas. Congreso presencial (English version below) En los últimos años, el terror ha experimentado una renovada visibilidad cultural. El éxito del cine reciente, la consolidación de una auténtica edad de oro de las series televisivas y la aparición de nuevas voces literarias, impulsadas también por el trabajo de editoriales especializadas, evidencian que el horror ocupa hoy un lugar central en el imaginario colectivo y mantiene una extraordinaria capacidad para dialogar con las preocupaciones estéticas, sociales y políticas de cada época. Sin embargo, esta vitalidad cultural no siempre ha encontrado un correlato equivalente en el ámbito académico. Aunque en las últimas décadas los estudios sobre el terror han crecido de forma significativa, todavía persiste un amplio espacio para profundizar en sus implicaciones filosóficas y en los múltiples cruces entre el pensamiento, la literatura y el cine. Con el propósito de contribuir a este campo de investigación, el congreso Estética(s) del horror: filosofía, cine y literatura busca reunir a especialistas interesados en explorar las múltiples relaciones entre el terror y la reflexión filosófica, así como sus manifestaciones en la literatura y el cine. Nos interesan tanto los trabajos que analicen la filosofía del terror -sus categorías estéticas, éticas, metafísicas o políticas- como aquellos que descubran el terror dentro de la propia tradición filosófica, examinando la presencia de lo monstruoso, lo ominoso, el trauma o el horror en autores, problemas o corrientes del pensamiento, desde la Antigüedad hasta la filosofía contemporánea. El congreso aspira, así, a constituirse en un espacio interdisciplinario de diálogo en el que confluyan perspectivas filosóficas, literarias y cinematográficas para pensar el terror no como un género marginal, sino como una herramienta privilegiada para comprender las inquietudes fundamentales de nuestro presente y de nuestra tradición intelectual. El congreso Estética(s) del terror: Filosofía, cine y literatura dará la bienvenida a propuestas relacionadas con alguno de los siguientes ejes temáticos: Filosofía del horror/Estética del horror Horror e intermedialidad Horror y sociedad El congreso está organizado por el grupo de investigación ESCON (Estética contemporánea: arte, política y sociedad) del Departamento de Filosofía y Sociedad de la Universidad Complutense de Madrid (España), por el proyecto UCM 2026 "Historia Conceptual del Tiempo. Crítica y Política" (PR10/26-32656), y por el Grupo Grite (Grupo de Investigacion en Terror) de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (Argentina), tendrá lugar los días 3 y 4 de diciembre de 2026 en la Facultad de Filosofia (edificio A) de la Universidad Complutense de Madrid. Las propuestas de comunicación deberán enviarse a [congresoesteticasdelhorror@gmail.com] hasta el 11 de septiembre de 2026, indicando en el asunto del mensaje: "Estéticas del horror". Cada envío deberá consistir en un único archivo en formato PDF que incluya: Un resumen de la propuesta de hasta 300 palabras. Una breve nota biográfica del autor/a (máximo 150 palabras), con indicación de su afiliación institucional, en su caso. Se aceptarán propuestas en castellano o en inglés. Las comunicaciones tendrán una duración aproximada de 20 minutos. La notificación de aceptación será comunicada a los participantes antes del 30 de septiembre de 2026. Rafael Carrión Arias es Doctor en Filosofía y Doctor en Teoría de la Literatura y Literatura Comparada. Es profesor en el Dpto. de Filosofía y Sociedad en la Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM) y miembro del Seminario Nietzsche Complutense. Es autor multiples artículos de investigacion, así como de dos monografías: "Historia de la literatura griega: los orígenes del método genealógico en F. Nietzsche" (Peter Lang, Nueva York, 2020) y "Batman and the Shadows of Modernity: A Critical Genealogy of Contemporary Hero in the Age of Nihilism" (Routledge/Taylor&Francis, London, 2025). Fernando Gabriel Pagnoni Berns es Doctor en Artes y doctorando en Historia. Es profesor en la Facultad de Filosofía y Letras de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (Argentina), donde dicta cursos sobre cine de terror internacional. Dirige GRITE (Grupo de Investigacion sobre el terror) y el proyecto "Civilizacion y barbarie en el cine de terror argentino" y es autor de una monografía sobre la serie española de televisión Historias para no dormir (Universidad de Cádiz, 2020). Ha editado, además, volúmenes dedicados al bicentenario a los cineastas James Wan, Wes Craven y Dario Argento, al giallo italiano (University Press of Mississippi), al cómic de terror (Routledge) y sobre el terror báltico. Asimismo, dirige la colección Terror: Estudios Críticos (Universidad de Cádiz), la primera colección académica en España dedicada exclusivamente a los estudios sobre el género de terror. Call for Papers Aesthetics of Horror: Philosophy, Film, and Literature In-Person Conference In recent years, horror has experienced a remarkable cultural resurgence. The success of contemporary horror cinema, the consolidation of what many have described as a new golden age of television series, and the emergence of new literary voices-supported in part by the work of specialized publishers-all attest to horror's central place in the contemporary cultural imagination and to its enduring capacity to engage with the aesthetic, social, and political concerns of each historical moment. Yet this cultural vitality has not always been matched by an equivalent level of scholarly attention. Although horror studies have expanded considerably over the past decades, significant opportunities remain for further exploring the philosophical dimensions of horror and the many intersections between philosophy, literature, and film. With the aim of contributing to this growing field of research, the conference Aesthetics of Horror: Philosophy, Film, and Literature seeks to bring together scholars interested in examining the manifold relationships between horror and philosophical inquiry, as well as its manifestations across literature and cinema. We welcome contributions that address the philosophy of horror-its aesthetic, ethical, metaphysical, or political dimensions-as well as papers that identify horror within the philosophical tradition itself, examining the presence of the monstrous, the uncanny, trauma, or horror in philosophers, philosophical problems, or schools of thought, from Antiquity to contemporary philosophy. The conference aims to provide an interdisciplinary forum for dialogue in which philosophical, literary, and film studies perspectives converge to explore horror not as a marginal genre, but as a privileged lens through which to understand some of the most pressing concerns of both our contemporary world and our intellectual tradition. Topics The conference welcomes paper proposals addressing (but not limited to) the following themes: Philosophy of Horror / Aesthetics of Horror Horror and Intermediality Horror and Society The conference is jointly organized by ESCON (Contemporary Aesthetics: Art, Politics and Society), a research group within the Department of Philosophy and Society at the Complutense University of Madrid (Spain); the UCM 2026 research project Conceptual History of Time: Critique and Politics (PR10/26-32656); and GRITE (Research Group on Horror) at the University of Buenos Aires (Argentina). The conference will take place on 3-4 December 2026 at the Faculty of Philosophy (Building A), Complutense University of Madrid. Submission Guidelines Paper proposals should be submitted to congresoesteticasdelhorror@gmail.com no later than 11 September 2026, with "Aesthetics of Horror" as the subject line. Submissions should consist of a single PDF file containing: An abstract of no more than 300 words. A brief biographical note (maximum 150 words), including the author's institutional affiliation, where applicable. Proposals may be submitted in English or Spanish. Accepted papers will be allocated 20 minutes for presentation. Applicants will be notified of the outcome of the review process by 30 September 2026. Organizers Rafael Carrión Arias Rafael Carrión Arias holds PhDs in Philosophy and in Literary Theory and Comparative Literature. He is a Lecturer in the Department of Philosophy and Society at the Complutense University of Madrid (UCM) and a member of the Complutense Nietzsche Seminar. He is the author of numerous scholarly articles and two monographs: History of Greek Literature: The Origins of the Genealogical Method in F. Nietzsche (Peter Lang, New York, 2020) and Batman and the Shadows of Modernity: A Critical Genealogy of the Contemporary Hero in the Age of Nihilism (Routledge, 2025). Fernando Gabriel Pagnoni Berns Fernando Gabriel Pagnoni Berns holds a PhD in Arts and is currently completing a PhD in History. He teaches at the Faculty of Philosophy and Letters of the University of Buenos Aires (Argentina), where he offers courses on international horror cinema. He is the director of GRITE (Research Group on Horror) and of the research project Civilisation and Barbarism in Argentine Horror Cinema. He is the author of a monograph on the Spanish television series Historias para no dormir (University of Cádiz, 2020). He has also edited volumes devoted to the bicentenary of Frankenstein; to the filmmakers James Wan, Wes Craven, and Dario Argento; to the Italian giallo (University Press of Mississippi); to horror comics (Routledge); and to Baltic horror. In addition, he serves as the general editor of Horror: Critical Studies (University of Cádiz), the first academic book series in Spain devoted exclusively to horror studies.

items.title: Artificial/Ancestral: Black Theatre and the Question of AI
items.excerpt: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these tec...
items.fullDescription: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these technologies have arrived without history, entering an empty landscape awaiting innovation. Yet Black theatre has long grappled with questions of representation, embodiment, archives, intellectual inheritance, collective memory, labor, and futurity. Rather than asking simply what AI can do for Black theatre, this issue invites contributors to consider what Black theatre reveals about AI itself: its assumptions, limitations, aspirations, and consequences. Volume 4.2 of the Black Theatre Review seeks essays, interviews, case studies, pedagogical interventions, archival investigations, artist statements, and process reflections that place Black theatre and performance studies in critical conversation with artificial intelligence and related technologies. We are particularly interested in work that moves beyond questions of adoption, utility, or rejection toward deeper examinations of power, ethics, governance, memory, embodiment, and knowledge production. We welcome contributions from scholars, artists, archivists, educators, practitioners, dramaturgs, designers, and cultural workers whose engagement with these questions emerges from both theory and practice. The issue is organized around five interrelated areas of inquiry. These themes are offered not as rigid categories, but as points of departure for further investigation. Taken together, these areas encourage contributors to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a site through which questions of labor, memory, embodiment, governance, spirituality, and future-making can be reconsidered. AI, Labor and Extraction: The beneficiaries of AI systems, whose labor makes them possible and required forms of accountability when Black creative work becomes data. Possible points of investigation may include: The labor of artists whose knowledge underlies any AI-readable record and what ethical stewardship of that labor requires. Generative AI in dramaturgy, script analysis, and design workflows, and models of artist-led intentional integration. Archives, Memory, and Black Theatre Histories: How do AI systems shape, distort, recover, or fail to capture Black theatrical histories and modes of remembering? Possible points of investigation may include: Digitization and AI-training projects involving Black theatre collections and their assumptions about what counts as trainable data. AI-assisted archival misreadings, flattening, erasure, and historical distortion. Embodiment, Liveness, and Performance: What happens when embodied, communal, and improvisational performance practices encounter technologies built on prediction, simulation, and abstraction? Possible points of investigation may include: Case studies of AI in the classroom, rehearsal hall, or production process. The complementary offerings of embodied, ensemble-based theatre training to university-wide AI adoption. Relatedly, how do such offerings get recognized, funded, or institutionally protected? Ancestral Intelligence, Spiritual Knowledge, and Black Futures: Understanding AI as a knowledge system entering into conversation with much older Black diasporic traditions of intelligence, memory, and futurity Possible points of investigation may include: AI as ancestral intelligence, or Black diasporic traditions of pattern recognition, forecasting, memory, and knowledge transmission. How do Black diasporic understandings of knowledge, memory, inheritance, ritual, and collective survival shape the technological futures we imagine? Refusal, Governance, and Alternative Technological Practices: Forms of resistance, opacity, governance, and the possibilities of misuse Possible points of investigation may include: How Black artists are bending, breaking, or refusing AI against its intended use. Teaching against technological inevitability. Photograph, Visual Media, and Digital Project Documentation tBTR welcomes photographic, visual media, and digital project documentation that illuminates the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We encourage submissions featuring productions, rehearsals, classroom projects, design processes, digital or hybrid performances, archival initiatives, community-based projects, and artistic experiments that engage the themes of this issue. Submissions may include production photography, design renderings, screenshots, interface documentation, archival images, process documentation, and other visual materials that help narrate how artists, scholars, educators, and institutions are critically engaging AI and related technologies. All submissions must include the project or production title, names and roles of key collaborators, location, creator and/or photographer credit, date, and a 2-3 sentence description explaining the work's relationship to the issue's focus on labor, archives, embodiment, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, ancestral knowledge, refusal, governance, or Black futures. Contributors are responsible for securing all necessary permissions and reproduction rights prior to submission. Please contact the managing editor for additional information. Book Reviews, Performance Reviews, and Notes from the Field, and Multimedia Works In addition to scholarly articles, tBTR seeks book reviews, performance reviews, multimedia works, illustrative case studies, and notes from the field that engage the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We are particularly interested in contributions that document pedagogical experimentation, archival initiatives, institution-building efforts, production processes, dramaturgical and design practices, community engagement, and artist-led technological interventions. We also welcome reflections on the ethical, political, and aesthetic questions surrounding AI, including issues of labor, extraction, memory, embodiment, governance, ancestral intelligence, resistance, and alternative technological futures. Submission Guidelines The last date for submissions is September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT. Please refer to the tBTR website for specific article section guidelines. Manuscripts must be submitted in Microsoft Word using standard formatting (1-inch margins, double-spaced, single-column layout, and 12-point Times New Roman font). Please include an abstract and a 150-word author biography with your submission. All submissions must include footnotes and a bibliography and must fully comply with The Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), using the notes and bibliography system. Please do not use the author-date citation system or another style guide. Please upload your complete manuscript through the journal's online submission portal via the website. Early submissions will receive preference in the review and publication process.
