items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. Selection criteria include intellectual rigour, theoretical sophistication, methodological clarity, engagement with Vietnamese and Southeast Asian contexts, and relevance to symposium themes. Authors should remove identifying information from the abstract document prior to submission Submission portal: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Symposium format: The symposium will have a hybrid format. An additional online session will be held for online participants. KEY DATES: Abstract submission deadline: September 15, 2026 Notification of acceptance: October 2026 Full text submission: November 20, 2026 Symposium: December 10, 11, and 12, 2026 Symposium Venues: -December 10, Online -December 11, RMIT Unviersity, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam -December 12, Fulbright University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Abstract submissions: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Please submit the abstracts through the submission system. *Some users encountered problems while using Safari browser. If you have problems with registering, please use a different browser. Registration details to be announced. Please contact the organising committee for queries regarding accessibility requirements. The organizers plan to publish an edited monograph containing expanded, selected articles submitted to the symposium. Details to be announced. items.fullDescription: The erotic is a point of infinite signification, a navel in humanity’s symbolic circuit. However, despite its resistance to formalization, it is always in the process of not being written. As Octavio Paz insists, the erotic is a metaphor indelible to the human. As such, it is unsurprising that the manifestations of the erotic in subjective embodied experience are variable and correspond to equally plural treatments of it across the academic panorama. This diverse archive is bound by certain distinguishable threads, in terms of the potentiality of the erotic, its singular relation to language, and to the sphere of sexuality.

items.location: Kalamazoo, Michigan · International Congress of Medieval Studies
items.excerpt: This session invites 20-minute papers that attend to the partial and resistant ways queerness and transness emerge in medieval archives. Torn pages, smudged images, misplaced marginalia, and fragmentary traces all signal forms of queer archival participation. In reimagining archival potential how might medievalists access, interpret, or refuse archival le...
items.fullDescription: This session invites 20-minute papers that attend to the partial and resistant ways queerness and transness emerge in medieval archives. Torn pages, smudged images, misplaced marginalia, and fragmentary traces all signal forms of queer archival participation. In reimagining archival potential how might medievalists access, interpret, or refuse archival legibility? Contributions may address explicitly socio-political queer identities and communities, as well as approaching the archive itself as a site structured by both queer and trans abundance and absence. The session welcomes interdisciplinary approaches that reconsider how scholars encounter, interpret, preserve, and reimagine archives beyond inherited frameworks of organization, memory, and scholarly proximity. As queer and trans studies continue to reshape medieval scholarship, this session asks how archival methodologies themselves might be reconsidered. Building on Brian Schram's claim that queerness offers "a potent antidote to the oppressive regimes of categorization," the panel explores how queer and trans approaches challenge normative systems of preservation, legibility, and historical interpretation. The session is timely in its emphasis on archival structures, silences, and fragmentary traces as sites of inquiry, encouraging medievalists to think critically about how archives produce, obscure, or resist categories of identity, memory, and power. Abstract length: 300 word limit

items.fullDescription: Human machine interfacing can be as simple as pressing a button or as complex and entangled (also entangling) as inserting a brain chip into the skull. science fiction. Humans with implants, prosthetic and hybrid humans with electronic and mechanical extensions are yet another level are no longer science fiction. Yet, human-machine interfacing has started long before the invention of these technologies. Machines did communicate with us and tell us about themselves even before chatbots were invented. The clanking of a hammer on the anvil tells us that it is old and dull. The whistle of a microwave tells us that dinner is ready. The process of interfacing is not a one-way process. Through it, humans also communicate with the machine.

items.fullDescription: As some institutions restructure academic priorities in response to various pressures in higher education, the Humanities can face contraction, marginalization, or elimination. These challenges are intensified at specialized universities, meaning institutions oriented toward fields such as STEM, health sciences, business, etc., where Humanities courses are often kept to general education requirements and could be perceived as peripheral to students’ professional training. Within such environments, Humanities faculty must navigate not only broader disciplinary challenges but also institutional cultures that may misunderstand or underappreciate the field’s contributions.

items.fullDescription: If American mass media is an ecosystem, we cast the press as predators, and the celebrity as their prey. We envision the reporters grouped in a posse, arranged for an ambush. Camera flashes crack as they capture their quarry. By now, these perceptions have become truisms that obscure our own role as consumers in a matrix of violence, spectatorship, and stardom. If we condemn the paparazzi for their alleged violence, we also continue to revise and revisit their heyday in the age of print media. This seminar seeks papers that explore how violent desire—of the spectator, the press, the star – shaped the profusion of tabloid and true crime print culture across the Americas.

items.fullDescription: Conference online (via Zoom) CFP: What makes us happy and content in our life? Some people may point to fabulous fame, fortune, or money. Others may argue that interpersonal relationships are the key to happiness. But what if someone is alone? Is loneliness truly disastrous? Are there any benefits of loneliness? Can loneliness become an epidemic? To address these questions, this event focuses on a wide range of specific issues. We are interested in exploring all aspects of loneliness, both in the past and in the present-day world. The conference is intended as an interdisciplinary event. Hence, we invite researchers representing various academic disciplines: sociology, psychology, psychiatry, philosophy, anthropology, gender studies, literary studies, theatre studies, film studies, consciousness studies, social policy, cognitive sciences, and history, among others. The aim of our conference is to provide opportunities for researchers from a range of disciplines and countries to share their research, create an academically challenging and productive space for discussion, and enable them to establish long-lasting, ever-growing scientific networks and contacts with professionals worldwide. We welcome submissions from both experienced scholars and young academics at the beginning of their careers, as well as doctoral and graduate students. We also invite individuals interested in participating in the conference as listeners, without giving a presentation. The topics of the conference include but are not limited to the following suggestions: 1. Loneliness and Society loneliness and social relationships (in families, marriages, partnerships, workplaces, etc.)? loneliness and war loneliness and illness loneliness and self-isolation, social distancing loneliness among children loneliness among seniors the lonely crowd loneliness in urban spaces loneliness as an epidemic loneliness and pandemic loneliness and social exclusion (social class, racism, gender factors, educational status) loneliness and social media (Facebook, Instagram, etc.) 2. Loneliness and Culture loneliness in different parts of the world loneliness and religions loneliness and initiation rituals lonely communities abandoned nations expelled minorities loneliness and digital cultures / virtual communities the cultural taboo of solitude vs. hyper-individualism migrant loneliness and diaspora experiences 3. Individual experiences loneliness during self-isolation, quarantanne, loneliness as a state of mind loneliness and emotional isolation loneliness and depression loneliness and shame creative loneliness loneliness as a rest situational loneliness existential loneliness loneliness, aloneness, and solitude the commercialization of loneliness (the "rent-a-friend" industry, monetized companion apps, dating algorithms, and AI relationships) synthetic companionship & AI (digital intimacy, dating algorithms, and robotic care) 4. Literature and Arts loneliness in literature, film, theatre and visual arts lonely artists aesthetics, spaces, and narratives of isolation (e.g., in pop culture, life-writing, and architecture) Please submit abstracts (no longer than 300 words) of your proposed 20-minute presentations, together with a short biographical note, by 18 September 2026 to: lonelinessconference@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: Poster session at the conference "Entangled Normativities in the Digital Transformation: Technology, Society and the Shaping of Law" Present your research where law, technology and society are being negotiated. How much technological change can normative orders gover? How do law, ethics and social norms change themselves once their creation, mediation and enforcement become digitally mediated? No single discipline settles these questions. With a poster you discuss your project at the centre of the programme, alongside scholars and practitioners working on exactly these questions: Möllers (HU Berlin), Nassehi (LMU Munich), Paulus (former Justice of the German Federal Constitutional Court), Schlögl-Flierl (German Ethics Council), Foblets (MPI for Social Anthropology), Vec (University of Vienna), Hansen (State Data Protection Commissioner of Schleswig-Holstein) and Bubnys (European Commission), among others. What you get:Viisibility in front of leading scholars and practitioners rather than in a parallel session; substantive feedback in conversation plus a short written comment on your abstract; a citable peer-review process; networking with doctoral researchers from across Europe; free attendance on both days. Potential poster publication on our website. Who can apply. Doctoral researchers in law, science and technology studies, sociology, political science, philosophy and ethics, history, computer science and engineering with a societal research question, design, communication and media studies, and further or interdisciplinary fields. What matters is not your disciplinary label but your contribution to the relationship between normativity and technology. Your stage of doctorate is irrelevant: proposals, early outlines and first interim findings are as welcome as work nearing completion, and practitioners pursuing a doctorate alongside their work are invited too. From big picture to concrete cases. We welcome conceptual and foundational contributions (theories of normativity under technological change, legitimacy and the rule of law in digital governance, the interplay of legal, ethical, social and technical norms, automation of norm application, interdisciplinary methodology) as well as specific, applied and empirical work (the AI Act and data protection law in practice, platform regulation, digital administration and courts, predictive policing, health data, technical standardisation, sustainability, and case studies of individual technologies, authorities, decisions or regulatory processes). Please relate your contribution to one of the three guiding questions: (1) To what extent is technological change amenable to normative and in particular legal governance? (2) To what extent must normative orders, above all the law, themselves change? (3) What potentials and risks does the technological transformation of normativity and law entail? How it works. Each session opens with lightning talks: max. 90 seconds and one slide per poster; questions are taken at the posters rather than in the plenary. Day 1 (German, 5 November): pitch session 4:15-4:35 PM, poster session from 4:35 PM into the Apéro riche. Day 2 (English, 6 November): pitch session 11:20-11:40 AM, poster session 11:40 AM-12:35 PM before lunch. Posters are on display both days; your poster language determines your pitch day. Peer review and selection. Each anonymised abstract is assessed independently by two members of the review committee, with divergences discussed in the committee. Criteria: thematic fit, academic quality, originality, clarity, and potential to spark discussion in an interdisciplinary audience. All applicants receive a briefly reasoned decision by early October 2026; interdisciplinary submissions are read by reviewers from different fields. Poster. A0, portrait, printed and brought by you. Recommended: two or three key messages, body text at least 24 pt, a large self-explanatory title, and more visuals than running text - your poster should be understandable within a few minutes even when you are not next to it. Questions: lst@sot.tum.de. We look forward to your application!

items.fullDescription: This virtual seminar takes its inspiration from Saidiya Hartman’s citation of the Greek etymology of the word chorus : “to dance within an enclosure.” For Hartman, the chorus also furnishes a paradigm for thinking—to play on Jean-Luc Nancy’s notion—Black (non)being singular plural. In Wayward Lives , Hartman suggests that any of the minor figures can stand in for the others, not as a claim of homogeneity, but rather as a contention that their singularity can be read as paradigmatic of waywardness—in its queer heterogeneity—in general. The chorus of black femme and queer youth is thus at once a singular plurality and a plural singularity as they make beautifully riotous lives within the enclosure of social death.

items.location: Houston, Texas · American Comparative Literature Association
items.excerpt: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literatur...
items.fullDescription: Please consider submitting to the ACLA seminar titled "South-South Literary Relations and the Remaking of World Literature" by September 21, 2026 . You can submit your abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/cfp/70fe7418-c14a-468d-be1d-809e878f2e00/submit-paper/46d872df-9512-49a7-89f7-8bc710370693 Abstract from the ACLA CFP: Since the rise of World Literature as a major field of inquiry, discussions of literary circulation have often privileged routes that pass through metropolitan centers, emphasizing translation into dominant European languages, global publishing networks, and institutions located in the Global North. Yet literary works have long traveled through alternative circuits that connect regions of the Global South directly, producing histories of exchange that challenge center-periphery models of cultural transmission. This seminar invites papers that examine literary relationships among Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean, SWANA, Oceania, and other locations within the Global South. Such relationships may emerge through translation, political solidarity, migration, anti-colonial movements, publishing networks, educational institutions, shared aesthetic projects, or indirect forms of influence. They may also involve moments in which Northern institutions, languages, or markets facilitate, mediate, redirect, or constrain South-South encounters, raising questions about whether these exchanges can ever be understood as entirely autonomous. Rather than treating the Global South as a unified category, the seminar seeks to explore its internal heterogeneity, asymmetries of power, and competing visions of solidarity. How do texts travel between Southern contexts? What historical, linguistic, and political conditions make these encounters possible? What role do translators, publishers, periodicals, archives, and digital media play in creating or sustaining South-South literary networks? How might these circulations reshape concepts such as influence, comparison, translation, reception, or worldliness? We especially welcome papers that interrogate the implications of South-South literary exchange for the study of World Literature itself. If literary circulation is not exclusively organized through Northern centers, what alternative maps of World Literature become visible? Can South-South networks offer different ways of imagining literary value, canon formation, and global comparison? By foregrounding overlooked routes of circulation and exchange, this seminar aims to reconsider how World Literature is conceptualized and to illuminate the multiple worlds through which literature moves. Possible topics include, but are not limited to: South-South translation; comparative studies across the Global South; Cold War and Non-Aligned literary networks; postcolonial and decolonial approaches; migration and diaspora; publishing and periodical cultures; digital literary circulation; transregional modernisms; indigenous and vernacular exchanges; reception studies; archives of literary solidarity; and new theoretical approaches to World Literature.

items.fullDescription: Although internet culture may have brought about the hashtag #WeirdGirlLit,” women authors have long used writing to explore taboo and forbidden topics deemed beyond the purview of polite/patriarchal society. While Heather Colley of Writers Digest has noted that “Women in literary fiction are becoming murderers, cannibals, psychopaths, and stalkers,” we contend that female protagonists have long been unhinged both across time and space. Historically, freaky (anti)heroines have served as a release through which women readers could escape the restrictive confines of ideal femininity and instead probe hidden desires and other illicit aspects of their identities.

items.fullDescription: “We are now in the middle of a deep and decisive moment towards a more disciplinary, authoritarian kind of society,” says Stuart Hall in his speech for Human Rights Day in 1979 (78). He proceeds to explain the components and manifestations of this “crisis,” which eventually morphs into a drive for more “Law and Order” (79). If that was the middle, are we at the end of the crisis? Our daily experiences prove otherwise, as the drive for more Law and Order keeps us in a chokehold. We seem to be in a perpetual global crisis in which we watch global systems of justice like international law and the International Criminal Court deteriorate in front of our eyes, while capitalist and genocidal systems globally continue to thrive and strengthen their hold.

items.title: ACLA Online Panel: Case Studies in Feeling: Toward New Theories of Emotion Across Media
items.excerpt: Emotions continue to attract critical attention across disciplines. Scholars have noted the growing prominence of emotion in media, politics, and internet culture, which some describe as an "emotionalization" of social life (Yanacek 2026). Over the past three decades, emotion theory has provided a multidisciplinary lens for understanding literary and cult...
items.fullDescription: Emotions continue to attract critical attention across disciplines. Scholars have noted the growing prominence of emotion in media, politics, and internet culture, which some describe as an "emotionalization" of social life (Yanacek 2026). Over the past three decades, emotion theory has provided a multidisciplinary lens for understanding literary and cultural texts, phenomena, and movements. Brian Massumi's distinction holds that emotion is socially coded and contingent on language, whereas affect is a pre-linguistic, asignifying intensity that exceeds discourse's capacity to fully capture it (1995). Sara Ahmed reframes emotion as social and relational rather than private, arguing that emotions "stick" to bodies and objects through repeated circulation, accumulating or losing affective value in the process (2004). Historians such as Barbara Rosenwein instead approach emotion diachronically, investigating the sanctioned "emotional communities" of different historical periods and how their norms of feeling and expression changed over time (2006). These frameworks are not fully reconcilable. For example, Massumi's model of pre-personal intensity has been challenged by critics such as Ruth Leys (2011), who question whether a truly pre-social affect is theoretically or empirically defensible. This tension among circulation, historicization, and the limit of pre-linguistic feeling remains a live and generative debate in the field. Game studies extend this inquiry into interactive media, asking scholars to account for procedure, system, and player agency alongside representation when studying emotion in play and design. Meanwhile, recent advances in facial recognition and artificial intelligence have pushed machines "from analytical processors to emotionally perceptive entities," if not to emotional entities themselves (Slimani 2026). These approaches resist treating emotion as ahistorical, private, or apolitical. Studying feeling as a legitimate, theorizable object reveals how power operates through affect, opens texts to modes of engagement beyond decoding, and invites us to reconsider the boundaries of the human, including where those boundaries fall in relation to nonhuman and machine forms of feeling. This panel invites papers that develop, test, or complicate existing theories of affect and emotion through close case studies, rather than merely applying them. We welcome submissions on any literary or cultural form, including but not limited to novels, poetry, drama, film, and video games, from any historical period and geographical region. This panel will be held online. Please go to https://www.acla.org/seminars, log into your ACLA account, find the panel, and submit your paper proposal by clicking the submit button.

items.title: Across Borders, Across Texts: Echoes, Revision, and Rewritings in Black Literature
items.location: University of Houston, Houston, Texas. · American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA)
items.excerpt: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literatur...
items.fullDescription: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literature across centuries, dating back to the antebellum. For instance, "Flight to Canada" by Ishmael Reed and "Kindred" by Octavia Butler; Harriet Tubman's "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" and Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad, published almost two centuries after Incidents; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Percival Everette's 2024 "James." These examples reinforce the notion that newer Black literature echoes, borrows, and imitates seminal literatures. This seminar thus seeks to investigate how Black literary and cultural productions have imitated other, earlier literary productions, even across genres and geographical boundaries-like what the editors of the anthology The Negro Caravan (1944) called "a sort of literary inbreeding which causes Negro writers to be influenced by other Negroes…" Even Kwame Anthony Appiah recently aver that "the history of art is the history of people borrowing and adapting techniques and tropes from earlier works." We seek papers that-using fictional and non-fictional Black writings and art-connect the past to the present-papers that explore "imitation," "influence," and "intertextuality" as central to Black literature and Black arts. Guiding questions to consider include, but are not limited to: What literary traditions have endured across generations, and how have they survived? What forms of continuity exist across Black literary history-Plantation to post-bellum literary and cultural productions, Africa to the Diaspora, across centuries, etc.? How do Black writers create new meanings from older texts? What role does memory play in Black literary traditions? How do contemporary writers preserve or challenge earlier literary traditions? How does Black literature reinvent its own past? What histories continue to shape Black literary expression? How do questions of race, identity, and freedom evolve across Black literary history? What earlier genres continue to influence Black literature today? How does Black literature balance tradition and innovation? What can earlier Black literature teach us about contemporary Black writing? Submit abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/defa99b9-6a8d-41ab-835d-2f1281fc3640 Session modality: Strictly in-person. Questions? Email: saadewumi@wisc.edu

items.title: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature (ACLA 2027, online)
items.excerpt: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world...
items.fullDescription: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world literature theories, considered as an effective tool to rethink contemporary authorship issues, it encourages at the same time proposals that aim to identify and deepen conceptions of the author coming from understudied historical and geographical contexts, thereby broadening the cultural horizon of Western reflections on the subject. Indeed, we are mostly used to considering authorship as a romantic notion, strictly linked to the paradigm of genius and individuality, the authority of which was famously questioned by twentieth-century literary theory-relying primarily on such celebrated thinkers as Barthes and Foucault-before re-emerging in the post-structuralist era. However, other historical periods and cultures have not necessarily applied the same theoretical paradigms nor followed the same critical trajectory (think about collaborative or anonymous authorship in the Middle Ages, as well as the lack of the rhetoric of genius in most Far Eastern literary traditions, to give just a few non-exhaustive examples). In our opinion, it is therefore important to rethink the notion of authorship in the light of these divergent traditions, especially to ensure a more complex and multi-focal approach to it in an increasingly globalized literary context. Even though theories of world literature have profoundly transformed the ways in which the critical field of literary studies is currently understood, we argue that, in fact, the crucial category of authorship has received comparatively little sustained attention within this debate. While effectively highlighting how substantial changes in the literary system have simultaneously reconfigured the author as a global cultural agent whose visibility depends on complex networks of publishing, mediation, and institutional recognition, the world literature perspective has less frequently questioned the Western theoretical framework of authorship as a productive and individual stance. We therefore suggest that merging genealogical reflections on authorship with world literature studies could help to make the latter much more inclusive and global, rather than a mere framework of Western concepts superimposed on the literatures of the rest of the world. We welcome papers in English, French, Italian or Spanish. Possible topics include: - authorship in world literature theories; - the intersection of authorship, postcoloniality, and the global literary market; - twentieth-century theories of authorship and their global afterlives; - pre-modern, indigenous, and non-Western conceptualizations of the author; - multilingual, exilic, diasporic, and transnational authorship. Please submit your proposal through the ACLA's online paper portal by September 22, 2026 (an abstract of no more than 1,500 characters and a short bio-bibliography). Once your account has been created, simply click on the "propose a paper" button available at the following link: https://www.acla.org/ seminar/263adf13-fe6c-4fc3- 95f7-87083b14e3f9. Should you encounter any difficulty, please do not hesitate to contact the seminar organizers (giovanni.salvagninizanazzo@ parisnanterre.fr; federico. ristagno@phd.unict.it). Notification of acceptance will be sent by December 1, 2026.

items.excerpt: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

items.title: TALKING DIFFERENTLY: MARGINALISED WOMEN AND THE FORMS OF INTERSECTIONALITY IN SOUTH ASIA
items.excerpt: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www....
items.fullDescription: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e Marginalised women in South Asia are read for what was done to them, far less often for what they made. This seminar asks what comparative literature can do about that. Intersectionality has become the default grammar for writing about marginalised women in the region. It arrived from a particular genealogy - Black feminist jurisprudence in the United States - into a region that had theorised compounded subordination for a century under other names: Phule on caste and women's education; Ambedkar on endogamy as the mechanism reproducing caste through control of women; Pandita Ramabai; Uma Chakravarti's Brahmanical patriarchy; Gopal Guru's claim that Dalit women talk differently; Sharmila Rege's Dalit feminist standpoint. Whether the import clarifies or flattens that inheritance is contested. Nivedita Menon argues that intersectionality serves states and donor agencies better than feminist politics; Sunaina Arya and Anandita Pan reply that the fault is citational, not conceptual. That argument has run almost entirely in social science. Our premise is that intersectionality is a diagram - a crossroads, a grid, a set of axes. Literary forms do not behave like diagrams. They work through voice, genre, meter, silence, obscenity, laughter, ritual and untranslatability. What does intersectionality look like as a reading practice rather than a taxonomy of identities? Where does form outrun the grid, and what should replace it - standpoint, assemblage, repertoire, abundance? Three provocations frame the seminar. First, the arithmetic of injury: criticism here tends to produce a tally of wounds, in which the Dalit, Adivasi, Muslim, trans, disabled or displaced woman is legible chiefly through what was done to her. Charu Gupta shows this figure has a history: in colonial Hindi reformist print the polluting "vamp" gave way to the deferential sufferer, Surpanakha displaced by Shabari, while the Dalit virangana of 1857 offered a rival image that never took. Following Gupta, Anjali Arondekar on archival abundance over loss, and Shailaja Paik on Tamasha performers who turn vulgarity into leverage, we welcome papers that read craft, expertise, pleasure and the ordinary. Second, marginality is not virtue. Tanika Sarkar's work on the Hindu wife as ground of cultural nationalism, and on women's agency inside right-wing movements, refuses to assume that subordination guarantees a critical position. We want dominant-caste women's self-writing - Rashsundari Debi's Amar Jiban - read alongside rather than apart from Dalit testimonio, and the complicities an axis model hides. Third, translation. Most of these texts do not exist in English. Bama's Karukku and Challapalli Swaroopa Rani's Telugu poems reach the Anglophone academy through an apparatus - glossary, preface, caste footnote, anthology - that turns literature into evidence. Swaroopa Rani's "Water" registers not only the village/wada line but the gradations within it, leather-worker and weaver. The grid has grids inside it, and translation is where they flatten. Topics might include, but are in no way limited to: the genre problem in Dalit women's testimonio; Dalit feminist poetry read as theory; the manufacture of the suffering woman in colonial print and the counter-archives that failed; nineteenth-century women's self-writing and its caste unconscious; women as agents of majoritarian politics; sung and seasonal repertoires as authorial economies rather than folklore; Adivasi women's poetry and the politics of script; landays and Afghan women's oral forms; testimonial method in Kashmir; plantation labour and memory in Sri Lanka; Muslim women and the meme as a genre of gendered communal violence; trans and hijra life-writing at the caste intersection; devadasi, Tamasha and courtesan archives read for abundance; caste in North America and Gulf labour circuits; translation as method. We invite papers on any South Asian language, region, period or diaspora. Researchers and Faculty Members at every career stage are welcome, including independent researchers and those working outside the Anglophone academy, and papers that argue against the seminar's premises are equally welcome. To submit: proposals go through the ACLA portal, not to the organisers directly. Visit https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e and use the "Propose a Paper" button. Current ACLA membership is required. Deadline 22 September 2026. We'd like to have you in person, please mention your preferred mode- ONLINE/IN PERSON along with the abstract. Enquieres: nandinigayen006@gmail.com; tamanna0602@gmail.com

items.fullDescription: In his book, Bioinsecurities: Disease Interventions, Empire, and the Government of Species (2016), Neel Ahuja's theory of "the body as a transitional theater of imperial warfare" explores how the control of human and nonhuman bodies proliferated the expansion of empire over the 19th century to the present. Despite the growing hegemony of biomedical control, there have always been and continue to be significant moments of resistance and agency in which marginalized (colonized/Indigenous) communities have challenged or reformulated/redefined the concepts of body, disease, and health. This seminar seeks to foster a discussion in order to understand how the body can be read as a transnational figure of resistance and refusal both in the 19th century and today. Through various disciplines on the subjective and untold experiences of the body, health(care), and illness, we hope to shed light on the fluctuations in imperial medical frameworks and decolonial epistemology that pose alternative narratives-both realist and speculative-about biomedical discourses of health, gender and sexual normativity, disability/deficiency, hygiene, humanness, life/death. We are interested in questions such as: How are illnesses phrased, represented, imagined in marginalized communities? How is the effectiveness of care and therapies a scientific, ethical, and cultural problem? How can the medicalized body-or the body that is made into a site of changeability and "treatment"-become a speculative site entangling place, race, gender, and sexuality? This seminar welcomes papers that take on interdisciplinary approaches to literature and other forms of cultural production such as film, print culture, and music that engage with the theme from the 19th- 21st centuries across the world. We are especially interested in lesser-known materials and understudied communities. Topics of interest include but are not limited to: Narrative medicine from all types of media Bioethics Biopolitics and governmentality Mental health and literature, art and media studies Limitations of medical or pharmaceutical knowledge Medicalization of health/illness Marginalized bodies in medicinal knowledge (queer, disabled, racialized, female) Community/Immunity Pandemic and contagion Aging studies and end-of-life care, childcare/youth studies Utopia/Dystopia/Ecotopia Toxicity and Waste Trauma and memory studies Supernatural bodies, cyborg and alien "others", metamorphosis and transformation (Digital) post-life, afterlife studies, martyrdom Animal studies, Post-humanism To submit an abstract, please go to: https://www.acla.org/seminar/82ccd196-900f-482d-aac6-3b983a0957b2. Click the "Propose a Paper" button.

items.title: Thinking in Images: Visualization, Imagination, and Empathy in Reading
items.excerpt: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a te...
items.fullDescription: Visualization and imagination have long been recognized as vital to the act of reading. While Russian Formalist Viktor Shklovsky may have denounced the maxim "Art is thinking in images" in his seminal essay "Art as Device" (1917), in favor of strategies of defamiliarization, mental images and imagery are some of the most important ways we engage with a text. In Dreaming by the Book , Elaine Scarry describes the function of poetry and novels as "instructions for mental composition" (244). That is, a text encourages readers to fill in the blanks; to reconstruct for themselves certain sensations, emotions, etc. These blanks, according to Wolfgang Iser in The Implied Reader , require readers to draw upon imagination, whereby meaning is created. Ultimately, literature encourages us to envision realities and modalities outside of our own. It is for this reason that reading fiction is considered to be an exercise in empathy--which Marco Caracciolo and Karin Kukkonen conceptualize to be a form of feeling with; of "imagining what we take him or her to be experiencing at a given moment" ( With Bodies: Narrative Theory and Embodied Cognition , 76). This seminar invites papers which attend to the function of visualization, imagination, and/or empathy in reading. In particular, participants are asked to consider how texts across a variety of genres, languages, time periods, cultural contexts, and subject positions, encourage similar or convergent ways of visualization, imagination, and empathy. Can we say reading is "thinking in images"? To what degree do texts encourage the generation of mental imagery and does this necessarily lead us to empathize? How does reading differ phenomenologically from engagement with other arts and mediums? What are the implications of cultivating an embodied and empathetic reading experience, particularly in an era of increasing polarization and automatization? How do certain texts reflect historical and cultural variations in bodily experience? We welcome interdisciplinary approaches drawing from affect theory, narratology, reader-response theory, phenomenology, psychoanalysis, cognitive literary studies, and other related fields. Possible topics may include, but are not limited to: Theories of mind (ToM) and cognitive approaches to reading; embodied models of reading. The impact of genre and form(at): fiction vs. non-fiction, literary vs. genre fiction, nonstandard/"non-literary" texts. Differences across bodies: gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, religion, and/or ability of readers, authors, narrators, and/or characters. Reading in translation or in different languages and effects on the ways we visualize, imagine, and empathize. Theories of imagination, literary imagination, and limits to imagination in reading. Narratological inquiries; impact of perspective and focalization impact on how we visualize and empathize. Reading in the age of Artificial Intelligence. How do AI/LLMs read and how do we read works produced by them?

items.title: ACLA SEMINAR: Becoming Monster: Representation and Rights
items.excerpt: American Comparative Literature Association IN-PERSON 2027 Annual Meeting (May 20-23, 2027), Houston, Texas Organizers: Dr. Julia Chan (Lingnan University) Fatma Betul Ciftci (Lingnan University) One is not born a monster; the monster is produced. From Beowulf to Ruthven to Dracula to cyborgs, 'monster' is a cultural construction, a humanly-produced non-h...
items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association IN-PERSON 2027 Annual Meeting (May 20-23, 2027), Houston, Texas Organizers: Dr. Julia Chan (Lingnan University) Fatma Betul Ciftci (Lingnan University) One is not born a monster; the monster is produced. From Beowulf to Ruthven to Dracula to cyborgs, 'monster' is a cultural construction, a humanly-produced non-human. This seminar invites scholars to discuss the monster both as a literary figure and as the representation and construction of a cultural and political identity. Through this, it aims to explore the question of where, why, and how monsters are produced, and what these monsterized creatures "show" about the communities that "produce" them. The seminar discusses how theory, from Freud's "the uncanny" to Cohen's "monster theory" to Creed's "monstrous feminine," can help us understand monsterization. The monsterized body is pushed outside the category of the "human" and thus outside the status of a rights-bearing subject. In this respect, monsterization begs the question of rights. This seminar aims to understand and make visible how the process which "produces" the Other as a monster, works in relation to rights. In Of Monsters and Migrants, Peter Arnds traces this process through Carl Schmitt's concepts of sovereignty and the "state of exception" and Agamben's biopolitics: to monsterize the migrant, the stranger, the refugee allows one to push them outside the protection of the law. As Arnds shows, the question of who - and what - monsterizes is therefore also the question of who is, or is not, recognized as a rights-bearing subject. The second focus of the seminar is the reclamation of the monster. Susan Stryker's "My Words to Victor Frankenstein Above the Village of Chamounix" identifies the trans body with Frankenstein's creature. It reverses the accusation of the "unnatural," constructed body and transforms the words "monster" and "creature" into terms of power reclamation, self-representation, and resistance. The monster is not only a position produced by the powerful but also one that can be reclaimed by those who are monsterized. What else can we see in monsters beyond the gendered or racial Other? We encourage scholars working in different areas-literary studies, television, film and anime studies, law and human rights theory, postcolonial and critical race theory, queer and trans theory-to offer new definitions of, and reflections on, the category of the monster. We invite papers around the following questions: How does the monster negotiate who counts as "human" and who counts as a subject of human rights? What social, political, or legal aspects make a body a monster? What strategies do those who are monsterized use to reclaim their representations and rights? How do different media construct the relationship between monsters and rights? Submit your paper title and abstract through the ACLA submission portal on the ACLA website by September 22, 2026, and note that you must be logged in to see the "Propose a Paper" button. Link for the seminar: https://www.acla.org/seminar/43ce7d31-1cb1-46b8-a8a2-6d34614d1e5e

items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. ACLA Paper Submission link: https://www.acla.org/cfp/2b603883-5d9b-44ae-a485-c732ba80d4bf/submit-paper.

items.fullDescription: Over the last two decades, we have seen a surge of scholarship at the intersection of Food Studies and New Materialist theory. Thinkers like Elspeth Probyn (2000; 2016), Jane Bennett (2010), Annemarie Mol (2021; 2024), and Kyla Wazana Tompkins (2024) explore the diverse ways in which edible matter acts on our bodies, wills, and dispositions, in multilayered entanglements that involve water, minerals, fungi, bacteria, plants, as well as human and nonhuman animals. These material-discursive networks urge us to rethink not only our notions of agency but also our ways of being, knowing, and relating.

items.fullDescription: This call is for panelists to present on an approved in-person NeMLA 2027 panel on "The Gothic Servant." While the Gothic has long been associated with monsters, haunted houses, unstable hierarchies, and hidden knowledge, the servant's specific connections to the genre's core dynamics of space, affect, and plot have been critically undertheorized. Yet Gothic narratives fundamentally depend upon servant figures to produce narrative tension, mediate hidden knowledge, and expose the instability of domestic, social, and political order. This panel therefore positions the Gothic servant not as a supplementary character but as a central Gothic mechanism and epistemological problem worthy of scholarly attention and analysis. We invite panelists to consider the following types of questions: In what ways does the servant function as a Gothic mechanism, producing narrative tension, circulating forbidden knowledge, and exposing the instability of domestic and class order? How do the servant's social and/or affective roles (as caregiver, confidante, observer, jailer, etc.) shape Gothic plots and complicate power hierarchies within Gothic narratives? How does the servant's structural invisibility produce, rather than merely reflect, Gothic preoccupations with spectrality, repression, identity and/or power? Topics may include but are not limited to: servants as uncanny, spectral, or monstrous figures; servants as central to Gothic plot and narrative structure; servants, secrecy, and forbidden knowledge; race, coloniality, and servitude in imperial and postcolonial Gothic; invisibility and the Gothic politics of service; servant figures in contemporary Gothic; and the afterlives of Gothic servant characters in adaptation and other media. We welcome papers on servant characters in Gothic texts from the mid-nineteenth century to the present, from any geographical area. All abstract submissions must be submitted through the NeMLA portal. When doing so, please submit to panel 22348, "The Gothic Servant" (https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22348).

items.fullDescription: Historically, researching and teaching the different art forms took place in a well-sealed vacuum: for example, using literary theory to decipher one of the great texts, visual and compositional analysis to examine a sublime painting, or montage splicing to perceive the nuances of film. However, it is becoming more difficult to recognize the borders that separate cinema, literature, and the visual arts. Factors including the rise of globalized societies and the emergence of new technology have forced us to reconsider medium specificity and our relationship with creative expressions and works of art.

items.fullDescription: Inclusive teaching and digital accessibility are two important concepts that align with Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles; they move away from "retrofitting" (i.e., fixing a problem after a student struggles) toward a "proactive” design (e.g., building a system that works for everyone from the start). Inclusive teaching is a pedagogical framework that focuses on designing a learning environment where every student (regardless of race, gender, socioeconomic status, or learning style) feels valued and has an equal opportunity to succeed. Whereas digital accessibility is a technical standard that ensures that digital tools, documents, and platforms are usable by everyone, regardless of ability.

This panel seeks to raise questions about how contemporary Anglophone speculative fiction addresses the current cultural moment and issues like artificial intelligence, immigration and the internet’s dissolution of privacy. Formally, how do 21st century dystopian novels connect science fiction with realism? With magical realism?

items.fullDescription: What strategies can paper ephemera teach us in the digital age? This panel invites conversations by writing instructors, educators, poets, and artists exploring the work that happens at/within the margins of writing. Both literally and figuratively, we take an expansive scope to the term “margins,” imagining not only the writing that appears on the space of the printed page, but writing that would normally be scrapped, discarded, remixed, or ephemeralized. This can include digital ephemera, such as “disappearing” messages in Instagram or other communication services. At another angle: margins can also mean the liminality of writing, the furthermost edges of what’s often standard and visible.

items.fullDescription: This panel session seeks to explore the cultural fascination surrounding "The Backrooms," an internet 'creepypasta' about an abandoned office building with endless corridors that became a popular YouTube series and most recently, a blockbuster horror film. What are the Backrooms? Do they represent an artificial or alien intelligence attempting to simulate reality? Are they a glitch in the imperfect fabric of an unstable universe? Are they a metaphor for the subconscious, techno-paranoia, wasteland necrocapitalism, corporate control, or the internet itself? Or is this all just a retelling of the Greek myth of the Labyrinth for a Gen Z audience?

items.fullDescription: This roundtable discusses the convergence of literary expression and digital activism as means of empowering a community. The shift of passive representation to active agency in the 21st century can be common in the digital space where the local knowledge is stored and disseminated. We discuss how marginalized groups, namely Dalit writers and activists, have used digital humanities to evade authoritarian gatekeepers and develop transnational solidarities. This session welcomes people to talk about how online spaces can be seen as a form of regenerative space where the testimonios of Dalit can be heard, transforming the world into a supportive space of collective action and literary insurgency.

items.fullDescription: TITLE: Language Learning Beyond the Classroom: Virtual Exchanges, Platforms, and AI MODALITY: Hybrid: The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. CHAIRS: Liana Ewald (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Dagmar Jaeger (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) ABSTRACT: This session explores the growing role of virtual exchanges, commercial platforms, and AI-mediated interactions in language, literature, and culture courses. In recent years, many instructors have experimented with new ways of connecting students with speakers, authors, and communities beyond the classroom: Teletandem exchanges, Zoom conversations with writers and artists, commercial conversation platforms, and AI conversation partners. These exchanges can open up forms of communication and cultural contact that are difficult to create in a traditional classroom, especially for students who may not have access to study abroad or regular interaction with speakers from other linguistic and cultural contexts. At the same time, these tools raise important questions. What kinds of communities do these exchanges create? What changes when conversation becomes mediated through platforms or AI? How do students respond to the differences between speaking with another person and interacting with an AI system designed to simulate one? What happens when intercultural exchange becomes something organized and mediated by commercial companies, especially when those relationships may at times raise questions about inequality or exploitation? The session is especially interested in presentations grounded in classroom experience, as well as broader reflections on the pedagogical and theoretical questions raised by these forms of virtual and AI-mediated exchange. Possible topics include current and emerging forms of virtual exchange, AI-mediated interaction, commercial platforms, the changing relationship between human and technological forms of communication, and the pedagogical, cultural, and ethical questions these developments may raise in the years ahead. items.fullDescription: Drawing inspiration from Adrienne Rich's seminal book Of Woman Born (1976), in 2006, Andrea O'Reilly coined the term "Motherhood Studies" and established a new interdisciplinary academic field aimed at studying "motherhood" as an institution and "mothering" as an experience. O'Reilly emphasized the importance of adopting a feminist framework designed expressly for mothers: a "matricentric feminism" necessary for an intersectional exploration of motherhood. Within "Motherhood Studies," being or not being a mother matters, and the experience of motherhood is treated as a category alongside gender, class, and race.

items.fullDescription: As Sidonie Smith and Julia Watson argue, “autobiographical storytelling is a performative act through which narrators construct rather than simply describe selves.” In recent times, “life writing” has become a familiar term in literary and cultural studies, encompassing a range of written texts, including autobiographies, biographies, letters, memoirs, slave narratives, prison narratives, captivity narratives, travel narratives, confessionals, conversion narratives and even in recent times, personal diaries. However, rather than remain transparent records of lived experience, life writings actively shape identities, produce historical knowledge, preserve cultural memory, and intervene in social and political worlds.

items.fullDescription: The guiding thread of this panel develops around a curious remark by Jacques Rancière that would seem to amend a classically Aristotelian thesis: “man is a political animal because he is a literary animal,” the fundamental condition of which is the “excess of words” constitutive of the human animal’s politicalness. Literature (or poetry) has long been placed in close proximity to politics, as we find in Plato’s Republic , where philosophy and literature—and, more generally, philosophy and politics—turn out to be perennial adversaries.

items.fullDescription: In her resolute commitment to telling stories about Black life without the white gaze, Toni Morrison articulated a model of community empowerment grounded in local knowledge, intra-communal collaboration, and the self-reflexive narration of Black worlds. While Morrison remains one of the most visible public advocates of this aesthetic and ethical orientation, practices of Black worldmaking across African and diasporic literatures have long exceeded mere response to anti-Blackness. Even under conditions structured by racial violence, coloniality, displacement, and social rupture, Black communities have continually generated modes of life, relation, memory, and imagination that assert the possibility of worlds otherwise.

items.fullDescription: Panel Proposal for the NeMLA Convention, Newport, RI, March 6–9, 2027 Planetary crises—climate change, toxic pollution, biodiversity loss, and energy transition—are profoundly uneven in their distribution. Their material consequences are shaped by infrastructures of class, race, colonial histories, state power, and global capitalism. Increasingly, literary, artistic, and cultural texts across the world foreground these asymmetries, framing ecological crisis not only as environmental catastrophe but as a question of justice: Who breathes polluted air? Who profits from green transformation? Who consumes melting ice? Who bears the social and environmental costs of planetary change?

items.fullDescription: How do writing and general education programs create conditions for communities that empower themselves-sustaining, growing, and often exceeding their original design? This panel invites papers that examine collaborative relationships among students, near-peers, tutors, and faculty that form in and around writing instruction and beyond, with particular interest in work that attends to the unexpected: encounters, connections, and forms of growth that arise when pedagogy exceeds the transactional to become genuinely communal. Papers might address-for example-embedded tutoring or near-peer mentoring in composition; teaching-and-learning communities (communities of practice) among faculty, tutors, and students; writing or Gen Ed programs at HSIs, HBCUs, or open-access institutions; the relationship between first-year instruction and identity transformation; intergenerational writing communities and alumni engagement; or the challenges that AI poses to authentic intellectual and creative development. Empirical, theoretical, and reflective approaches are welcome, as is work that bridges composition pedagogy, approaches to general education, and literary (or other forms of) community-building.

Yet the fantasy of constructed or quasi-human life long predates modern computing and robotics. Classical and pre...
items.fullDescription: "Did I request thee, Maker?": Contemporary Cyborgs and Androids and Their Pre-Modern Antecedents Contemporary speculative fiction is saturated with androids, cyborgs, artificial intelligences, and technologically engineered forms of sentience. Yet the fantasy of constructed or quasi-human life long predates modern computing and robotics. Classical and pre-modern literature repeatedly imagines artificial beings, animated matter, virtual persons, mechanical servants, enchanted automata, and forms of life that blur the boundary between the human and the non-human. This panel invites papers that place contemporary representations of manufactured or technologically mediated beings in dialogue with their classical or pre-modern antecedents. Possible pairings might include science fiction, film, television, comics, anime, or video games alongside texts from antiquity through the early modern period. What conceptual, philosophical, theological, or aesthetic frameworks for artificial life emerge in pre-modern literature? How do earlier traditions of animation, embodiment, enchantment, or mechanical simulation anticipate contemporary debates surrounding AI, consciousness, labor, gender, race, affect, or personhood? While Frankenstein remains a central touchstone for discussions of artificial life-and itself invokes Paradise Lost as part of that genealogy-this panel is especially interested in less frequently discussed genealogies and archives. What ancestors to the android or cyborg might be found in Ovid's Metamorphoses, the works of Shakespeare, medieval romance, alchemical traditions, Jewish mysticism, Islamic philosophy, Buddhist narrative traditions, or other non-Western pre-modern texts? Possible topics may include automata and animated objects; artificial or manufactured bodies; alchemy, magic, and technological imagination; pre-modern theories of mind, soul, and consciousness; race, gender, and constructed embodiment; virtuality, simulation, and illusion; labor and mechanical life; monstrosity and the posthuman; game studies and worldbuilding; and theological or philosophical anxieties surrounding creation itself.

items.fullDescription: In the definition given by Podnieks, matrifocal literatures are written and narrated by mothers in the first-person or limited third-person voice, rendering maternal identity and experience from subjective perspectives. Such narratives (re)value the significance and meaning of maternal figures in cultural, social, and national arenas, and often contest or negotiate traditional ideologies of the “good” mother as self-sacrificing, nurturing, and sexless with her antithesis, the “bad” mother. In the last few years, we have seen the rise of matrifocal writings published to break taboos about previously silenced reproductive experiences, create a sense of community, support, and care, and, overall, empower people.

items.fullDescription: Haryanvi Dalit theatre occupies a highly marginalised position within the broader landscape of Indian theatre. It may aptly be described as “the marginalised among the marginalised,” as it has remained largely excluded from both mainstream theatre studies and Dalit cultural historiography. Haryanvi Dalit Swang theatre was active long before the Dalit Panther Movement, but it received little attention due to its lack of publication and translation into English. This book seeks to recover, document, and critically examine the neglected legacy of Haryanvi Swang, with particular emphasis on its Dalit traditions and practitioners, thereby contributing to a more inclusive understanding of Indian theatrical heritage.
