The aging Vincent Chang built his career playing bumbling Japanese soldiers and one-dimensional Asian stereotypes in classic Hollywood. He’s confronted by the up-and-coming Bradley Yamashita, who insists that Asian (American) characters should be played with dignity and accuracy. The heart of the play is an ambivalence about Asian (American) representation and whether viewers should sympathize with Chang for taking the only acting jobs available or with Yamashita in his condemnation of the racist roles—or with both.

items.fullDescription: Cultural Studies and Media Studies / Interdisciplinary Humanities This seminar opens up discussions on past and ongoing debates around indigeneity and indigenous lives. In America, the aboriginals assumed the title "First Nations" to distinguish their identity from that of the non-indigenous people. Historically, the European colonizers have classified the tribes for the sake of academic interest, colonial justification and administrative purposes. The British in India developed criminal ethnography archives and aspired to have systematic anthropometric methods to identify so-called 'criminal tribes'. Native Americans in America were placed in reservations where their natural habitat was controlled, and residential schools adopted the government's ideology, restricting their ability to express themselves. Indigenous communities from across the world have undergone experiences of exploitation, un/under-compensated coercive displacement, and asymmetrical access to socio-economic resources. The economic transformation of indigenous societies following colonial interventions has been shaped by historical and contemporary dynamics, influencing their livelihoods, right to resources and autonomy, and has led to disruption of their social structures. When navigating beyond their organic territory, the aboriginals often experience abuse, culture shock, and erosion of traditional knowledge due to forceful assimilation. Referring to ethnographic exploits and documentary filmmaking, Lynda Jessup points out that ethnographic text-making of indigenous lives can run counter to "an ideology claiming transparency of representation and immediacy of experience." When viewed in the context of contemporary critical anthropology, such artworks symbolize ethnographic authority based on Western masculine subjectivity. Paper topics include (but are not limited to): Ø Government projects and indigenous/aboriginal/tribal economy Ø Cultural hybridity and culture shock in Indigenous narratives Ø Epistemological Shifts in Indigenous Studies - Interdisciplinary Approaches Ø Empowering Indigenous communities - Future Scopes and Limitations Ø Artworks on Indigenous Lives and the Question of Ethics Ø Indigenous Population, Migration, erosion of Traditional Knowledge Ø Indigenous societies as fostering a culture of sharing and sustainability Ø Totemism, ancestor-worship, indigenous performative rituals

items.location: Rhode Island · Salve Regina University in Newport,

The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal e...
items.fullDescription: The digital infrastructure in today's world mirrors the colonial administrative structure with its control over data, policing user's behavior, and pushing narratives for the majoritarian political power. The global tech giants have as much sway in geopolitics as the global leaders themselves. Previously the conditions of colonization created an unequal economic infrastructure that marginalizes the local communities, and even after independence from the colonial power, the trade relations remain that of a colonial appendage. Similarly, the upkeep of the digital sphere is not without its economic and environmental hazards. Anibal Quijano (1928-2018) a Peruvian sociologist, talks about the plight of this expansion for resources in his book, On the Coloniality of Power. He says: …the contemporary scientific community, insists on destroying the conditions for life on the planet. So, both the movement of the most subjugated people in this world, those who would not be able to exist if they sold their means of subsistence, and those who realize that if all this comes to an end no one will be able to survive, come together in a shared analysis. 359 He stresses on the role of the communities who've resisted the colonial and postcolonial measures to protect their land, water, and air over the years. It shows how the communities have more of a lateral structure which allows for debate and discussions as opposed to the hierarchy of the colonial administrative infrastructure. This panel seeks to garner discourse around the digital world's ambivalent nature of enhancing global communications and generating jobs at the cost of endangering local communities. Questions, challenges, and possible solutions for a community-oriented resistance will be among the many concerns discussed at this panel. Submit on NeMLA's website: Submit an Abstract

items.fullDescription: Conference: 2-4 December 2026, in Gdansk, Poland and online CALL FOR PAPERS: In our modern world, which some have argued to be disjointed while immersing itself ever deeper in crisis, the turning back to "the olden days" and the ensuing nostalgia constitute anoticeable phenomenon, both individually (the memory of biography) and collectively (the memory of history). Another important - and equally noticeable - phenomenon is the longing for something vague, indefinite or never existent. Hence, during our interdisciplinary conference we would like to concentrate on the phenomena of nostalgia and melancholy. We are interested in all expressions of longing forthe past, from the reassuring and action-propelling ones to those which paralyze us, leading to despair and utter dejection. We aim to explore the experience of nostalgia and melancholy in its multifarious manifestations: psychological, social, historical, cultural, philosophical, religious, economic, political, artistic, and many others. We will also devote considerable attention to how these phenomena appear and transform in artistic practices: literature, film, theatre, and visual arts. This is why we invite researchers representing various academic disciplines: anthropology, history, psychology, psychoanalysis, sociology, politics, philosophy, economics, law, literary studies, theatre studies, film studies, memory studies, nostalgia studies, migration studies, consciousness studies, dream studies, gender studies, postcolonial studies, medical sciences, psychiatry, cognitive sciences, design, project management and other disciplines. items.fullDescription: Across contemporary literary and cultural studies, increasing attention has been devoted to the ways in which geological matter shapes cultural imagination, environmental memory, and literary form. Rocks, minerals, fossils, sediments, ruins, and other more-than-living material formations are no longer understood merely as settings or symbols, but as archives of deep time, environmental change, historical violence, and planetary entanglement. This panel invites papers exploring how literature engages with the Earth as a site of memory, relation, and meaning-making. We are particularly interested in approaches that examine geological formations, landscapes, material traces, planetary archives, and sedimented histories as participants in literary and cultural processes rather than passive backdrops to human experience. Possible topics include geologies of memory; deep time and literary temporality; environmental trauma and material archives; fossils, ruins, and traces; sacred landscapes and earth-based imaginaries; extraction, waste, and environmental justice; posthumanist and new materialist approaches to literature; relational poetics; and the intersections of geology, ecology, and cultural memory. We welcome contributions addressing literary and cultural texts from any historical period, linguistic tradition, or geographical region, as well as comparative and transnational perspectives. The session will be held in-person but a few remote presentations may be included. Please clearly indicate in your submission whether you wish to participate in person or remotely. All abstract submissions must be submitted through the NeMLA portal https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22630. items.title: Perceptions du féminin entre Orient et Occident, de la marginalisation à l'empowerment
items.excerpt: À travers le temps et l'espace, les femmes ont traversé différentes transformations, visibles et invisibles, qui les ont tour à tour élevées au rang d'êtres divines, de saintes vénérées et de guérisseuses indispensables, ou reléguées au statut de sorcières, épouses du diable et véritables épreuves imposées aux hommes sur cette t...
items.fullDescription: À travers le temps et l'espace, les femmes ont traversé différentes transformations, visibles et invisibles, qui les ont tour à tour élevées au rang d'êtres divines, de saintes vénérées et de guérisseuses indispensables, ou reléguées au statut de sorcières, épouses du diable et véritables épreuves imposées aux hommes sur cette terre. Ces représentations ne sont pas anodines. Elles sont le reflet d'un ordre social qui, selon les époques et les cultures, a utilisé l'image de la femme comme miroir de ses peurs, de ses désirs et de ses contradictions les plus profondes. Partant de ce constant, nous nous posons une question centrale : dans quelle mesure les perceptions du féminin ont-elles conditionné la capacité des femmes à s'emparer de leur propre pouvoir d'action, à construire des espaces d'autonomie, et à devenir des actrices actives du changement au sein de leurs communautés ? En comparant l'Orient et l'Occident, en traversant les siècles et les frontières culturelles, nous proposons d'examiner comment ces figures, la sorcière, la sainte, la guerrière, la guérisseuse, ont simultanément servi d'instruments de contrôle social et de vecteurs d'une puissance féminine que les sociétés patriarcales ont rarement su nommer sans la craindre. Car derrière la sorcière brûlée se cachait souvent une femme savante. Derrière la sainte célébrée, une communauté qui avait besoin d'une femme forte pour survivre. Derrière la guérisseuse marginalisée, un savoir collectif protégé. Cette table ronde invite des propositions qui mobilisent une approche historique de longue durée, attentive aux continuités et aux ruptures, tout en proposant de nouvelles méthodes et de nouveaux outils pour l'étude de ces représentations, toujours vivantes, toujours agissantes, dans les sociétés contemporaines. Comment ces figures du passé résonnent-elles avec les débats actuels sur le genre, le pouvoir, et l'empowerment des femmes ? Comment les communautés d'aujourd'hui héritent-elles, consciemment ou non, de ces imaginaires ? Les propositions, en français ou en anglais, ne doivent pas dépasser 300 mots. Les propositions sont à soumettre via le portail:https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22550

items.title: Silences as Resistance in Public Narratives
items.excerpt: Silences as Resistance in Public Narratives Silence is generally seen as something to surmount: we break silence; we give voice to silenced stories; we speak out against injustice. But silence can be a powerful mode of expression in its own right. There is a history of silent protest. Silence can reject dominant expectations or refuse to offer up a story...
items.fullDescription: Silences as Resistance in Public Narratives Silence is generally seen as something to surmount: we break silence; we give voice to silenced stories; we speak out against injustice. But silence can be a powerful mode of expression in its own right. There is a history of silent protest. Silence can reject dominant expectations or refuse to offer up a story for voyeurism, appropriation, or commodification. It can push reader-listeners to listen for something wordless, to play an active role in striving to understand, and simultaneously to recognize the limits of their ability to understand another person's trauma. Silence is rarely ever singular. This seminar, building on successful past seminars about the roles and limits of narrative silences, examines how silences function as forms of resistance to injustice and trauma. It asks: how can we use silences (as creators or as audiences) to create new spaces-spaces of care, of resistance, of justice? How do we listen to what silences have to say-in fictions, testimony, activism, artistic forms of witness, our classrooms and institutions? How can audiences attend to silence in ways that promote structural change? Participants may choose to address some of the following questions: How do the forms of silence change between public narratives (e.g. testimony or activism) and works of art and literature? How can we theorize silence as a narrative framework? How do we hold the tension between listening to silence, on one hand, and the necessity of speaking out against injustice, on the other? How do historical and geographical contexts change the types or effects of silences that strive to oppose injustice? How can we keep from homogenizing silences and attend to them in their specificity and situatedness? Papers on all genres, media, geographical contexts, and languages welcome. Please submit 200-word abstract and bio through the NeMLA portal to Kelly Minerva and Lisa Propst.

items.fullDescription: Call for Proposals NeMLA's 58th Annual Convention - "Empowering Communities" March 6-9, 2027 | Salve Regina University, Newport, Rhode Island Roundtable Title: Writing and Wellbeing: A New Urgency for Human-Centered Composition Pedagogies Primary Area / Secondary Area: Rhetoric & Composition / Pedagogy & Professional Modality: In person only Chair: Miranda Lutyens, University of Massachusetts Amherst College is a time of excitement and novelty, but it can also bring about anxiety and uncertainty. Those unsettling emotions have been on an upward trend in recent years, with a host of factors - the fallout of the pandemic, social media's curation of idealized lives, and existential fears relating to climate change, generative AI, and political turmoil - raising concerns about the wellbeing of students. The college writing classroom has a long history of offering compassion through creative (and even countercultural) approaches to teaching and learning. This included affirming the rights of linguistically marginalized students to their own language, as well as efforts to keep struggling writers in school to keep them out of the Vietnam War. As we collectively face new urgencies, this roundtable session invites participants to share research projects and instructional practices that consider college writing classrooms as affective and embodied spaces. Recognizing concerns such as instructors' emotional labor and under-resourced writing programs, the session primarily focuses on putting forward innovative approaches to making writing instruction responsive to students' experiences in increasingly uncertain times. Insights gained from critical teacher research on human-centered pedagogies are particularly welcome, as are contributions from all levels of writing instruction, including first-year composition, writing in the disciplines, writing support for graduate students etc. The goal of this roundtable is for both participants and attendees to leave with expanded perspectives on how the college writing classroom might offer students more pleasure and new possibilities - to reimagine a more salutary relationship to writing, to engage with the written word in more personally meaningful ways, and to gain a greater awareness of themselves and others. The roundtable also aims to offer practical strategies for enacting - or at least experimenting with - new classroom practices. Submission Deadline: September 30, 2026 Please submit abstracts via the NeMLA portal: https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22547 Convention information can be found here: https://www.nemla.org/convention.html

items.title: Cripping Literary and Cultural Studies: Neurodivergent and Mad Methodologies
items.excerpt: Critical disability studies and the medical humanities have generated growing interest within cultural and literary studies in the past decade. Yet scholars in these fields tend to engage with disability and illness either thematically, examining their representations in literary and cultural productions, or rhetorically, tracing how they inflect the very...
items.fullDescription: Critical disability studies and the medical humanities have generated growing interest within cultural and literary studies in the past decade. Yet scholars in these fields tend to engage with disability and illness either thematically, examining their representations in literary and cultural productions, or rhetorically, tracing how they inflect the very form of these productions. Rarely do such approaches ask how disability and illness might transform criticism itself, that is, how neurodivergent or mad cognition might become a critical resource, transforming the ways we read, analyze, and inhabit literary and cultural studies. This panel invites papers that take up this question, exploring what new methodologies neurodivergence and mental illness-including, but not limited to, autism, ADHD, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, OCD, PTSD, and depression-can generate. How might neurodivergent and mad ways of thinking and being-in-the-world produce innovative, crip approaches to literary and cultural analysis that refuse sane- and neuronormative standards? Such a project finds grounding in Arseli Dokumaci's concept of disability-as-method, "a creative approach through which research methods are informed by, modeled after, and tailored to the situated knowledges of disabled people" (Activist Affordances, 11). It also resonates with Robert McRuer's call to challenge "straight composition, with its demand for composed and docile texts, skills, and bodies" (Crip Theory, 171), as well as with Jack Halberstam's notion of low theory, a voluntarily undisciplined mode of knowledge that defies the linearity and restraint of established academic discourse (The Queer Art of Failure). We welcome papers that generate or point toward new critical approaches grounded in neurodivergent and mad cognition and cripped methodologies. We particularly encourage submissions in which such cognition is presented as an embodied epistemological standpoint where neurodivergent or mad experience shapes the work from within, rather than serving as a structuring metaphor.

items.title: Between Mobility and Mobilization: Lessons from Cultural Production
items.excerpt: In what ways can literary mobilities provoke questions about social movements and forms of resistance in the current global order? Mobility is not simply the physical navigation of spaces, but an embodied and affective act with deep socio-cultural and political significance. Literary and cultural work that represents varied forms of mobility can reveal co...
items.fullDescription: In what ways can literary mobilities provoke questions about social movements and forms of resistance in the current global order? Mobility is not simply the physical navigation of spaces, but an embodied and affective act with deep socio-cultural and political significance. Literary and cultural work that represents varied forms of mobility can reveal contradictions between the exercise and assumption of agency and uneven historical and social conditions of restriction. Whether mobilities are framed as environmental, diasporic, colonial, or decolonial, they pose questions about material and symbolic conditions of power that dictate who can move and in what ways. This session welcomes proposals on subversive mobilities in cultural production to interrogate the connections between mobile subjects and wider mobilization efforts, resistance movements, protest cultures, and expressions of dissent. In investigating the links between mobility and mobilization, this session seeks to engage a wider conversation about the relationship between movement and resistance. Central questions this session will address include: How do different narratives-literature, film, graphic and visual arts, or other forms of storytelling-connect mobilities to activism and resistance movements? How do narrative forms participate in protest cultures? How do mobilities articulate political claims? This session welcomes papers with interdisciplinary approaches to narrative forms and textual cultures.

Fundamentada no pensamento decolonial e em abordagens interdisciplinares críticas, a sessão examina como essas comunidades desafiam as estruturas coloniais que continuam a moldar a produção de conhecimento, as práticas institucionais e a representação cultural no mundo contemporâneo. O painel acolhe contribuições que investiguem as interseções entre decolonialidade, educação, justiça epistêmica, resistência cultural e agência comunitária em diversos contextos geográficos e históricos. Os tópicos podem incluir, entre outros, pedagogias decoloniais, ensino superior e desigualdade social, produção de conhecimento baseada na comunidade, linguagem e poder, diáspora e identidade, memória e resistência, exclusão racializada, epistemologias indígenas e africanas, perspectivas feministas e interseccionais, migração, mídia e ativismo cultural. Ao abordar o tema da convenção, "Empoderando Comunidades", esta sessão busca criar um espaço interdisciplinar para discutir como comunidades marginalizadas reivindicam voz, visibilidade e autonomia por meio da educação, práticas culturais e formas alternativas de conhecimento. A sessão incentiva pesquisadores das áreas de estudos literários, estudos culturais, educação, ciência política, sociologia, estudos pós-coloniais, estudos africanos e campos afins a contribuírem com perspectivas inovadoras sobre as possibilidades de futuros decoloniais e empoderamento coletivo.

items.location: Salve Regina University, Newport RI and Zoom · NeMLA
items.excerpt: I want to be accepted by society…live in a world I don't have to hide in…make choices without being in constant fear of them destroying me or the ones I care about." (Ada, liberated TanakX5 robot, on her hopes and dreams. Alex + Ada, Book 11) Many contemporary and recent speculative fiction texts interrogate the questions of "making kin" wit...
items.fullDescription: I want to be accepted by society…live in a world I don't have to hide in…make choices without being in constant fear of them destroying me or the ones I care about." (Ada, liberated TanakX5 robot, on her hopes and dreams. Alex + Ada, Book 11) Many contemporary and recent speculative fiction texts interrogate the questions of "making kin" with companion species, including the companions humans might engineer and build to keep us company. In her Staying with the Trouble, Donna Haraway proposes reknitting the current order to address Capitalocene-generated problems of overpopulation and overconsumption. To survive, humans must extend their care and loyalty to other inhabitants of our shared planet, and co-construct knowledge -sympoeisis-with them. Haraway includes part-biological cyborgs in the potential so-called symbionts with whom humans should co-exist, but does not expressly include fully non-biologic, mechanical partners in her analysis. Yet, as part of the thought experiment enacted by speculative fictions of manufactured fellow beings, Haraway's prescription might be expanded to encompass sentient partners whom humans engineer and manufacture to keep themselves company. This roundtable invites papers interrogating speculative fiction solutions for expanding kinship relations to sentient non-biologic companions, whether embodied robots, virtual companions, or other. In other words, how does a particular creator of an imagined world envision expanding Haraway's Chthulucene era of "oddkin" to included fully artificial as well as natural companion species? And how do these artificial companions fare, that is, are the humans in their worlds able to embrace their right to equal standing and accord them rights?

items.title: Beyond Hegemony: Masculinities in World and Comparative Literature
items.excerpt: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity...
items.fullDescription: This panel examines how literary and cultural texts from diverse global traditions imagine masculinity not merely as an individual identity but as a relational and communal practice. In an era marked by migration, political polarization, social fragmentation, environmental crisis, and renewed struggles for collective empowerment, narratives of masculinity have become central sites through which communities negotiate belonging, responsibility, vulnerability, and resistance. While dominant models of masculinity have often been associated with hierarchy, authority, nationalism, and exclusion, contemporary world literatures increasingly depict alternative masculinities grounded in care, ethical responsibility, emotional openness, solidarity, and collective survival. Such representations challenge inherited structures of power while opening new possibilities for community formation and social transformation. This panel invites comparative and transnational approaches that explore how literary texts, films, cultural narratives, and other expressive forms construct, critique, or reimagine masculinities within local and global communities. Particular attention may be given to how gender intersects with race, class, migration, coloniality, religion, ecology, technology, and cultural memory in shaping collective identities and practices of empowerment. Situated within the broader concerns of World Literature and Comparative Literature, this session seeks to foster dialogue across regions, languages, and traditions while investigating how masculinities participate in the creation-or disruption-of empowered communities. We welcome papers addressing, but not limited to: Comparative constructions of masculinity across world literatures Masculinity and migration, diaspora, or displacement Literary representations of fatherhood, mentorship, and communal responsibility Masculinities in Global South literatures Masculinity and environmental or ecological communities Masculinity, memory, and post-conflict reconstruction Queer and non-hegemonic masculinities in world literature Masculinity and cultural resistance under authoritarian regimes Masculinity, religion, and collective belonging Masculinity and affect in contemporary global fiction

items.title: Revisiting the Great War: Women's Voices, Experiences, and Works
items.excerpt: Our session examines the importance of women as fictional characters, authors, and purveyors of legacies associated with the Great War of 1914-1918. It is hoped that we can bring a fresh critical light to this pivotal moment in world history. Too often, scholarly reflection on the Great War tends to focus military activity and various aspects of masculine...
items.fullDescription: Our session examines the importance of women as fictional characters, authors, and purveyors of legacies associated with the Great War of 1914-1918. It is hoped that we can bring a fresh critical light to this pivotal moment in world history. Too often, scholarly reflection on the Great War tends to focus military activity and various aspects of masculine performance. We would like to use a wider lens for our discussion of the Great War. Please note the very wide range of perspectives in this seminar: authors, characters, and context. More precisely, our reconsideration of the works, authors, and legacies of the Great War includes three directions: first, the examination of women appearing as fictional characters in this normally male-oriented thematic area; second, reflection on women writers, artists, and filmmakers engaged in representing the Great War; finally, establishing historical continuities deriving from the relationship between women and the Great War. The flexible methodology of this session includes the examination of novels, poems, paintings, photography, film, documentaries, memoirs, and memorials. A few suggestions for interpretative directions: · Recent critical directions on topics relating to women and the Great War · Non-European, global writing on the Great War · Themes of colonialism, migration, class, public health, punition, sexual violence, and race · The inclusion of documentary, archival, and any relevant internet materials · Presentations on "Women, New England, and the Great War" · The involvement of women in medical and public health issues during the Great War · Women in the Great War as represented in museums, local, national, and global media.

items.fullDescription: Call fort submissions "Conversations with the Dead: Excavation as Re-vision" Chair: Edvige Giunta, Kean University The session invites presentations of prose, poetry, and/or hybrid writing that “turn” to the dead—not for the purpose of elegiac reminiscence but to unsettle or dismantle notions of chronology, inheritance, and other forms of linear, unidirectional connection between the living and the dead. Writers who turn to the dead find that that past transforms the present through the very process of excavation: communities are remade in the turning. This session will examine what that practice looks like across genres such as intergenerational memoir, speculative memoir, investigative essays, and personal rewritings of myths.

"Recent scholarship on increasing global conflicts and ensuing health crises urgently demands an intercultural and interdisciplinary re-inscription of the the intersection...
items.fullDescription: This VIRTUAL panel invites papers on "Narrative Medicine and Community Empowerment in Asian and Arab Graphic Narratives" for NeMLA 58th Annual Convention to be held on March 6-9, 2027. "Recent scholarship on increasing global conflicts and ensuing health crises urgently demands an intercultural and interdisciplinary re-inscription of the the intersection of medical humanities with arts and cultures. Such growing interest evinces how artistic and cultural forms reshape the diagnosis of traumas and pathologies and propel new forms of narrative engagement that fosters deeper connections, communal care, and collective empowerment" (Atieh 2026). As a pertinent example, graphic and narrative medicine "diverts from the standardized language of established medicine discourse and clinical frameworks whose limitation eclipses" (Atieh 2026) the "collective experience" and "mutual recognition" (Charon et al., 2016) of pathologies, whether psychological, physical, social, cultural, or ecological. Graphic narratives are "exceptionally committed to the reconceptualization of accessibility and care as communal practices that depart from individualized framings of clinical guidance or neutralized or centralized resilience. In particular, the implementation of visual narration moves beyond the abstraction or exclusive rhetoric of clinical diagnosis to develop the aesthetics of somatic-experiential embodiment that aligns with a decentralized experience" (Atieh 2026) Graphic medicine then "corroborates a multimodal intervention in clinical medicine narrative that anchors categorization and measurement as standardized indicators for the diagnosis of illness or its remission. Ultimately, graphic narration unsettles the opacity of biomedical discourse and its exclusive language, and reclaims an experiential or relational language that fosters deeper connections, promotes care, and advances responsibility toward whole and multispecies communities" (Atieh 2026). In this regard, we invite papers that particularly address the perspectives of Asian and Arab graphic narratives on "decentering healthcare discourse and transferring authority to embodied and collective experiences of pathology" (Atieh 2026). The invited papers may illustrate how the shared experiences that underpin Asian and Arab graphic medicine mobilize an inclusive healthcare culture that advocates the agency of decentralized access and collective production of knowledge, and contribute to future formation. Possible topics can include, but are not limited to: - Breaking collective stigma and silence around pathology - Promoting affinities around pathology - Posthuman graphic narration and multispecies cooperation and survival - Graphic narration and multilingual accessibility - Graphic narratives on ecological precarity and possibility - Comics and climate change traumas - Graphic narratives and war traumas - Graphic access and medical education - Empathy Building -Clinicians/caregivers and patients' solidarity -Graphic narration and remission societies - Visual storytelling and health literacy - Recuperating patients' voices as story-tellers and story-listeners - Visibility and inclusion of migrant storytelling of trauma -Solarpunk graphic narratives Interested individuals are asked to submit an abstract of no more than 300 words (excluding abstract title) and a 100-word mini-biography. Submissions will only be accepted through the CFP address https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22530 Submission Deadline: September 30, 2026; Modality: Remote only Panel Chair: Majda R. Atieh; Sultan Qaboos University

items.fullDescription: DESCRIPTION : This panel examines how colonial regimes constructed, managed, and contested the category of "indigeneity" as a shifting site of power, governance, and resistance. Focusing on the Spanish colonial presence in Morocco (1859-1956) as a primary case, the panel situates indigeneity within broader imperial frameworks in which racial, legal, and cultural categories were continually redefined through encounters between colonial authority and local agency. ABSTRACT : This panel examines how colonial regimes constructed, managed, and contested the category of "indigeneity" as a shifting site of power, governance, and resistance. In alignment with NeMLA's 2027 theme, "Empowering Communities," the session explores how colonial and postcolonial communities are not passive subjects of imperial classification but active agents who negotiate, appropriate, and transform imposed identities. Focusing on the Spanish colonial presence in Morocco (1859-1956) as a primary case, the panel situates indigeneity within broader imperial frameworks in which racial, legal, and cultural categories were continually redefined through encounters between colonial authority and local agency. Drawing on approaches from colonial studies, postcolonial theory, and cultural history, the panel also invites comparative and interdisciplinary perspectives on how indigenous and marginalized communities engage with structures of power through resistance, collaboration, and strategic adaptation. Particular attention is given to the role of bodies, knowledge systems, and cultural representations-including medical, military, literary, and visual archives-in shaping colonial governance and indigenous responses. Rather than treating colonial categories as fixed, the panel foregrounds their instability and the ways in which communities actively participated in their transformation. Possible topics include colonial constructions of indigeneity; indigenous agency and resistance; community formation under colonial rule; colonial medicine, biopolitics, and governance; race, legal identity, and cultural categorization; archives and historical representation; decolonial and postcolonial approaches to indigeneity; gender and colonial power; nationalism and anti-colonial movements; comparative imperial frameworks; and contemporary reconfigurations of indigeneity and belonging. Interdisciplinary and comparative contributions are especially welcome.

items.fullDescription: Somewhere in Morocco, a woman wakes up before dawn to open her cooperative. Somewhere in Africa, a young entrepreneur pitches his logistics startup to investors who have never been to his neighborhood. None of these people would see themselves as leaders in the usual way. Yet, each of them is doing something important: they are changing the conditions of their communities from within. Across Africa, leadership is not waiting to be brought in, trained, or certified. It is already happening in markets, cooperatives, informal networks, diaspora remittances, and communal land agreements that existed before the modern state. Scholarship has often overlooked these practices as forms of leadership. Yet, these are legitimate, complex, and politically significant forms of collective action. Africa's recent history is troubled, layered, and full of setbacks. Between periods of forced dependency and moments of self-creation, societies have continuously negotiated their own change. Today, as African economies are rapidly growing, an old question returns: who holds power during this transformation, under what conditions, and for whose benefit? The term "empowerment" is common in development reports, corporate responsibility frameworks, and policy documents, but the communities it claims to help are rarely the ones that define it. This panel aims to view business leadership not as a technical or managerial issue, but as a site of power. We understand leadership in its broadest sense: not as something limited to boardrooms or institutional hallways, but as a practice found in cooperatives, informal markets, women's savings networks, youth entrepreneurial groups, diaspora investment networks, and communal governance structures that have existed for generations.To study business leadership in Africa is, in this sense, to study the very fabric of social change. We invite papers from management studies, development economics, gender studies, anthropology,etc. that engage with the following questions: Who leads, and at what cost? This panel does not treat Africa as a single story. It insists on the specificity of places, languages, and histories . Papers focusing on national or regional contexts are as welcome as comparative perspectives. Abstracts, in English or French, should not exceed 300 words. Proposals are to be submitted via the portal:https://cfplist.com/nemla/Home/S/22551

items.fullDescription: Despite possessing intersecting histories and languages, Latin American studies and Latinx studies have historically been treated as separate fields of study. This panel seeks to spark a dialogue between fields by exploring themes of transhemispheric and archipelagic solidarity in Latinx and Latin American literature and media. Throughout the past and present century, how have Latinx and Latin American media-literature, film, art, or other forms-constructed expressions of community in dialogue with each other? How do works from Latin America reverberate in Latinx cultural productions, and how do Latinx cultural productions influence Latin American media? How do these intersections challenge our notions of the borders, both theoretical and physical, between both territories? Literature, film, art, and other forms have a long history as modes of cultural preservation and empowerment, especially in Latin American and Latinx communities. What can we discover about these communities and their agency through a borderlands approach to Latin American and Latinx studies? While submissions from Latin American and Latinx studies will be considered, papers explicitly engaging in solidarities between the two disciplines will be prioritized. Submissions in English, Spanish, and Portuguese are welcome. Interdisciplinary projects are also encouraged.

items.title: The Classroom as Counter-Archive: Place-Based Pedagogies of Community Empowerment
items.location: Salve Regina University. Newport, Rhode Island · NEMLA
items.excerpt: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in produ...
items.fullDescription: Education is an ideal means of empowerment, for it enables students to take ownership of the historical and personal archives that stand for their communities. This panel regards the classroom as a privileged site of such empowerment-particularly for students from immigrant families-and seeks proposals on how to equip them to become active agents in producing their own interpretations of the cultural and spatial memory they share with their forebears. We draw inspiration from courses in which students articulate their personal, familial, and communal relationships with the tangible and intangible spaces of the city they inhabit: from their own homes to the streets they traverse daily, the buildings, neighborhoods, and monuments they encounter, and the individual and social practices that animate them. Setting their lived experience against the historical archives that purport to represent them, students produce analytical descriptions of urban space. Their work collectively assembles a shared repository of cultural memory - a "counter-archive" that weaves together place-based learning, immigration histories, and autobiographical narrative. In classrooms of diverse composition, this work empowers along more than one path. Immigrant students illuminate the place of their communities within the urban social fabric, while others discover-in their own projects and in those of their classmates-insights that transform how they perceive the city and their own identities in relation to it. We invite educators across languages, periods, and disciplines to share pedagogical projects and activities-assignments, archives, community-engaged work, digital repositories, creative and testimonial writing-that treat teaching as a practice of empowerment. We especially welcome contributions that reflect on the theory of change behind their work: when does a classroom project produce agency, and how do we know?

items.title: Resisting from the Edge: Marginal Characters and Collective Empowerment
items.location: Salve Regina University, Newport, RI · NeMLA
items.excerpt: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. items.fullDescription: This panel invites papers that examine the agency of marginalized characters in literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic productions from the French?speaking world across any historical period. Artistic works offer numerous examples of figures who maintain an ambivalent relationship to their communities. Because of their social or ethnic origins, their divergent perspectives, or their transgression of established norms, certain characters find themselves pushed to the margins of social, familial, or professional groups. While such exclusion may appear to weaken those who experience it, this panel asks whether marginalization might also function as a source of strength. Can marginality become a generative position? Do marginalized individuals succeed in forming new communities that enable them to confront stigma and ultimately overcome it? This discussion seeks to shift our understanding of the place occupied by marginalized individuals and groups in fictional narratives. By considering the networks of solidarity that emerge among marginalized subjects, the panel explores what lies beneath their presumed inferiority, inviting critical attention to what is hidden, erased, or rendered invisible within dominant narratives. More importantly, we will examine how marginalized communities may become empowering spaces of resistance, mutual support, and hope. Drawing on approaches from cultural studies, postcolonial theory, sociolinguistics, and intersectionality, this session seeks to understand how literary, visual, audiovisual, and artistic narratives stage the tensions between marginality and belonging, strength and vulnerability. Proposals engaging with environmental humanities, posthumanism, Indigenous studies, as well as diaspora and migration studies are strongly encouraged. We also welcome submissions drawing on gender and queer studies, memory and trauma studies, digital humanities, or other interdisciplinary frameworks within the humanities. We welcome proposals of 250-300 words, in French or English, submitted by September 30.

items.fullDescription: Despite the international prominence of Stanisław Lem and, more recently, Andrzej Sapkowski's The Witcher , Polish science fiction and speculative literature remain strikingly underrepresented in English-language scholarship. Existing criticism tends to orbit a small number of canonical figures and a handful of frequently revisited texts, leaving a rich, historically complex tradition, spanning censorship-era political allegory, post-1989 transformation, contemporary literary crossover, and a distinct national cinema largely unexamined outside of Polish-language scholarship.

items.excerpt: Public Humanities invites submissions for the upcoming themed issue Memorial Culture in Public Art, which will be guest edited by Rebecca Friedman and Alex Lichenstein. items.fullDescription: Public Humanities invites submissions for the upcoming themed issue Memorial Culture in Public Art, which will be guest edited by Rebecca Friedman and Alex Lichenstein. The deadline for submissions is October 15, 2026. Description Memorial Culture in Public Art invites submissions that examine the role that art of all kinds - ephemeral public art installations, performances, sculptures, murals, or permanent state-issued monuments - can play in the public's understanding of the past, present, and future. We ask contributors from a multitude of disciplines and from multiple global perspectives to consider how public arts can serve as collective mnemonic inspiration. We invite contributions from academics, public scholars, memory activists, and artists and creatives of all kinds, to explore the role of public art as a form of resistance as it contributes to collective, place-based memory in the face of forces from political ideology and spiritual expression to gentrification and cultural obliteration. Submissions can consist of academic articles, artistic interventions, interviews, dialogues, or other forms. Regardless of format or genre, contributors should engage with questions that include: How have regimes around the globe and across time, whether autocratic or democratic, created-or destroyed--narrative sites of collective memory in public spaces? How can individuals and groups intervene to transform nationalistic, colonial, or dominant narratives through their re-telling and/or transformation of art in public spaces? How can - and have in the past - individuals, groups, communities, neighborhoods, and even nations use(d) art, performance, and display to resist the power of erasure and cultural amnesia? How can public art help usher in a more equitable future based on reconstituting social memory? The current moment witnesses many struggles over memory, as emergent constituencies demand more accountability from public memorial culture while myriad regimes seek to obliterate it. This issue of Public Humanities seeks fresh and innovative approaches across time and spaceto consider these and other conundrums of memory activism and commemorative public art. The editors are especially interested in contributions from and/or about the Global South and the postcolonial world. By engaging the past through its present material and aesthetic manifestations, this issue of Public Humanities will use a host of disciplinary frames to explore how art and commemoration in public spaces open up a window onto how humans navigate space and time through artistic imagination, creativity and expression, and how collective remembering reflects and shapes our contemporary moment. Submission Guidelines Submissions should be written in accessible language for a wide readership across and beyond the humanities; see How to Write for Public Humanities. Articles will be peer reviewed for both content and style. Articles will appear digitally and open access in the journal. All submissions should be made through the Public Humanities online peer review system. Authors should consult the journal's Author Instructions prior to submission. All authors will be required to declare any funding and/or competing interests upon submission. See the journal's Publishing Ethics guidelines for more information. Contacts Dr. Rebecca Friedman | friedmar@fiu.edu Dr. Alex Lichtenstein | alichtens@gmail.com Questions regarding peer review can be sent to the Public Humanities inbox at publichumanities@cambridge.org.

items.fullDescription: "That Sounds Funny": CFP for ALA "Music and the American Literary Imagination" symposium The American Humor Studies Association (AHSA) invites submissions for a proposed panel for the American Literature Association (ALA) 2027 symposium "Music and the American Literary Imagination," to be held January 28-30, 2027, in Nashville, TN. For hundreds of years, humor has been an indelible element of American popular music as well as literature. This AHSA-sponsored, non-guaranteed panel seeks proposals that consider the connections between American humor, American music, and American literature. We invite submissions on any genre, period, or place, including papers that explore the fuzzy boundaries of what it means to be "American." We are especially interested in presentations that examine humor practices in the American South; for example, proposals might consider the use of humor in Southern rap, children's author Shel Silverstein's role in shaping the "outlaw country" sound, or the recent rise of right-wing "humorists" in Nashville. Together, the presentations constituting this panel will explore the pitfalls and possibilities of the imbrication of music, humor, and American literary culture. Please send a 250-word abstract and a brief biography by October 15, 2026, to AHSA Vice President Benjamin Schwartz at bs8959@princeton.edu. All panel participants must be AHSA members before the ALA conference opens on January 28, 2027. The Constance Rourke travel award is available for graduate students on a panel. The award varies between $100 - $300 (depending on AHSA funds and the number of applicants) to help defray the cost of attending conferences with AHSA-sponsored panels. We also remind everyone that AHSA has in place a mentoring program to help emerging scholars prepare an essay for publication. Presenting at ALA can be the first step to being published.

This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its...
items.fullDescription: European Comic Art Special Issue 'Francophone Graphic Narratives / Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance' European Comic Art invites proposals for a special issue on 'Francophone Graphic Narratives/Bande dessinée: Authority and Resistance'. This issue will examine how francophone graphic narratives engage with, challenge, and reimagine authority in its many forms - political, cultural, institutional, and aesthetic - and how they forge practices of resistance and dissent. The bande dessinée is a medium that subverts hierarchies and blurs boundaries. Long regarded as the lowly offspring of literature and the visual arts, comics have since been legitimised by scholars and artists demonstrating their capacity to engage with complex sociohistorical, political, and cultural topics. This 'Ninth Art' now occupies an increasingly important place in university classrooms, academic publications, and public discourse alike. Its multimodal features - panel layout, gutters, framing, braiding, and complex interplay between text and image - allow comics to stage and challenge authority in formally distinctive ways. This aesthetic vantage point makes comics a powerful medium through which to bring displaced, excluded, and silenced narratives into view. From Chantal Montellier's impressive four-decade oeuvre of political cartoons and graphic novels contesting racism, misogyny and totalitarianism to Jessica Oublié's Peyi an nou , which provides a counternarrative to state discourse on the BUMIDOM, the bande dessinée has often served to undercut official rhetoric. This special issue of European Comic Art seeks articles that examine how Francophone bandes dessinées engage with dominant institutions and discourses from theoretical and pedagogical perspectives. How do comics represent power and powerlessness? How do they respond to hierarchies that exist in various settings and communities? How do they decentre and challenge 'standard' language practices? Finally, how might comics be used pedagogically to help foster students' critical thinking skills and question institutional, political, and social discourses? Possible topics include, but are not limited to: Migration Ecocriticism Social justice and political activism Gender and sexuality Comics and memory studies Class, labour, and economic inequality Pedagogy and second language acquisition Nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and globalization Colonial legacies, decolonial resistance/critique Monolingualism, multilingualism, and language politics Official histories, counter archives, and silenced narratives Humour, parody, satire, and subversion Submission Guidelines Please submit a 500-word abstract with a short biographical note to Liana Pshevorska at lpshevorska@wesleyan.edu and Valentina Denzel at vdenzel@msu.edu by October 15, 2026. Informal inquiries are welcome. Decisions will be communicated in November 2026. The deadline for submitting full manuscripts is February 28, 2027. Articles should be in English, approximately 8,000 words, including images, notes, and bibliography. Contributors may include up to four images, which will be factored into the overall length of the article. Each image will be counted as approximately three-quarters of a printed page, based on an estimate 400 words per page. Please note that authors are responsible for obtaining copyright permission for all included images. Documentation of permissions should be submitted alongside the manuscript.

items.title: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities
items.excerpt: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative a...
items.fullDescription: Call for Papers: NANO: New American Notes Online (ISSN: 2160-0104) Special Issue 18: Exploring the Boundary Waters of the Blue Humanities Special Issue Guest Editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri and Dana Van Kooy Deadline: 16 October 2026 Publication: spring/summer 2027 Full CFP Details: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/home/cfp-plus-submissions-new The creative and scholarly work being done in the blue humanities has deepened our turn towards exploring waterways and boundary waters. The currents circulating through the blue humanities flow into and from myriad disciplines, including anthropology, biology, decolonial studies, feminist/queer studies, geography, history, indigenous studies, literature, music, performance studies, philosophy, and the visual arts. The cultural and theoretical inlets being carved out by work in the blue humanities have proven generative in terms of developing a distinctive metaphor-laden language, analytic methods like Kamau Brathwaite's theory of "tidalectics," and new ways of submerging ourselves in both historical and unprecedented questions about the water that is in and, as Rachel Carson notes in her famous title, "around us." For this special issue, we invite submissions of traditional and multimodal essays of up to 5,000 words (excluding works cited) that explore the boundary waters of the blue humanities. We encourage essays focused on narratives as well as submissions that explore art installations and other medial forms that address the boundary waters circulating around and through the blue humanities. Topics may include but are not limited to the following: Boundary waters that divide and connect nations, classes, and/or ecological zones Mythic, cinematic, and visual narratives of how humans and/or nonhumans are "held," migrate, or are moved through watery littorals Critical explorations like those associated with "tidalectics," a term that comes from Kamau Brathwaite, who proposed an alternative framework for literary and political engagement that is grounded in the rhythm of waves and the cyclic ebb and flow of tides "Portraits" of littoral space(s) in literature, history, myth, the visual arts, and theatrical and musical performances Exploring the significance of physical, structural, and emotional vulnerabilities and instabilities within littorals, shoals, or port cities Hydrological infrastructure (colonial, postcolonial, urban, rural) associated with port cities, canal locks, and dams Relational undercurrents that speak to our ways of submerging ourselves into the watery worlds that surround us Traditional water ways: ways of being with or "holding" water The role of inland waterways in routing stories and/or facilitating/impeding human and nonhuman migrations Exploring the agency of oceans and rivers in sustaining capitalist and imperial economies and their alternatives Water's many forms (snow, ice, fog, rivers, oceans) and ways "water" facilitates connection and/or imposes isolation How waterways-"paths" of water and ways of being with water-lead us to new or alternative futures Scenes of erosion that expose lost or forgotten histories Please direct questions to the special issue editors: Eric Denbang Kunkuri [edkunkur@mtu.edu] and Dana Van Kooy [drvankoo@mtu.edu] For questions about the use and disclosure of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, please see NANO's AI Statement (https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Journal-Information) Please use the Submission Form on top left of the CFP page: https://nanocrit.com/index.php/Submissions/Submission-Form NANO: New American Notes Online is a free, open-access, peer-reviewed journal. NANO does not charge for submission, review, or publication. It is indexed in the MLA International Bibliography, GALE, ProQuest, and DOAJ.

items.fullDescription: The rise of the superhero is one of the most significant cultural developments of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Since the debut of Superman in Action Comics #1 (April 18, 1938), superheroes have evolved from colorful comic-book figures into powerful global symbols that shape conversations about politics, morality, identity, technology, gender, race, mythology, trauma, and resistance. What began with the imaginative vision of Jerry Siegel (writer) and Joe Shuster (artist) has expanded into a worldwide phenomenon spanning comics, film, television, literature, gaming, digital media, and academic discourse.

items.fullDescription: Conference Theme: Beyond Repair: Reconciliations, Restorations, Resurgences Conference Dates: February 10-12, 2027 Submission Deadline: October 23, 2026 The African, African American, and Diaspora Studies Center at James Madison University invites proposals for its annual interdisciplinary conference Beyond Repair: Reconciliations, Restorations, Resurgences. The conference will be held from Wednesday, February 10 to Friday, February 12, 2027 and brings together scholars, archivists, and practitioners from a variety of overlapping and intersecting fields. Submit proposals by October 23, 2026. Repair has become one of the defining political and ethical vocabularies of our moment. Calls for reparations have generated new ways of imagining justice, accountability, and redress, while also raising questions about whether the language of repair is itself sufficient to address the enduring legacies of colonialism and slavery. This year's theme "Beyond Repair" gestures simultaneously in two directions: it evokes what may appear irreparable, but it also invites debate over what we mean by "repair" in the first place. What can it achieve? What are its limits? What lies past its horizons? What in our present condition is beyond repair, and where does this leave us for imagining a future that does justice to the past? This year's conference will be hybrid; we invite in-person and virtual presentations on all topics relevant to AAAD studies, even if not directly pertinent to the conference theme. We welcome proposals from scholars from all disciplines at any point in their scholarly careers. Proposals for individual presentations or pre-constituted panels could address, but are not limited to, topics such as the following: · Reparations and reparative structures · Post-conflict recovery · Frameworks of restorative justice · Relief and its discontents · Reconciliation and refusal · Resurgence and renewal · Community restoration · Global and transnational partnerships · Historical reckoning · Memory and forgetting · Archives and recovery · Narrative repair · Healing and health · Arts of restoration · Religious communities and social repair · Ecological restoration · Climate resilience · Land and belonging · Diasporic networks · Pedagogies of repair · Reproductive justice · Literary resurgences · Queer histories and futures · Transitional justice · Care and community · Reparative economy · Wealth and debt · Digital storytelling Please submit either a 300-word individual paper proposal or 1000-word panel proposal on the appropriate form linked below by October 23, 2026. Panel proposals must include at least three panelists. For panels, acceptance information will be sent directly to the panel organizer. Individual Paper Submission Form: https://forms.gle/rB6N9EB1MKNZAxBBA Panel Submission Form: https://forms.gle/5rCwccWXPFfxcgGw9 Further information and updates about the conference may be found at sites.lib.jmu.edu/aaadjmu. International respondents traveling to the United States in need of Visa documentation are encouraged to submit their abstracts as early as possible, ideally before September 15. International respondents will be notified on an ongoing basis after submitting their proposal. US respondents will be notified within a month after the deadline. Questions may be sent to aaadstudies@jmu.edu.

items.fullDescription: Call for Chapters Proposals Submission Deadline: July 17, 2026 Full Chapters Due: October 30, 2026 Submission Date: October 30, 2026 Introduction This edited collection features scholarly voices with attention to horror in its transmedia representations, including film, literature, comics, art, branding, and more. Chapters give attention to the ways that fans take up the realities and ideas presented in horror, the affordances of the genre, and participation in this network of storytelling. The reactions of readers/viewers/fans, the decisions of creatives, the presentation of ideas within particular forms of media, and more form elements of the researched conversation in this volume. Objective This collection seeks to advance conversation about the theoretical functions of horror across media including notions of adaptation and literary/literacy-based choices in the work. This includes, but is not limited to, design structures, cultural influences, the role of lore, (re)considerations of the monstrous, embodiment in the genre, sub-genre considerations, and more. Target Audience This book is intended for academics in media, literacy, literature, communication, and interdisciplinary fields. Students enrolled in courses in these fields can benefit from this knowledge as they pursue courses of study and further academic work in these disciplines. Recommended Topics Emotional and Philosophical Reactions to Horror Media Themes and Interactions across Media Representations in the Genre Adaptation Processes/Decisions/Designs in Horror across Media Studies of Narrative and Response/Interpretation Recent Trends/Movements in Horror Theoretical Approaches to Horror Composition/Representation Analysis of Race, Gender, Class in Horror Considerations and Reconsiderations of the Monstrous Author/Creator Decisions and Purposes in the Genre/across Media Horror Character and Author/Director Studies Critical and Analytical Work on Embodiment in Horror Critical and Analytical Examinations of Cultural Stories in the Genre The Role of Lore/Mythology in Horror Studies of Writing/Creating Processes in the Genre Fandom Communities, Fan Fiction, Cosplay, and Other Responses Submission Procedure Researchers and practitioners are invited to submit on or before July 17, 2026, a chapter proposal of 1,000 to 2,000 words clearly explaining the mission and concerns of his or her proposed chapter. Authors will be notified by July 31, 2026 about the status of their proposals and sent chapter guidelines.Full chapters of a minimum of 10,000 words (word count includes references and related readings) are expected to be submitted by October 30, 2026, and all interested authors must consult the guidelines for manuscript submissions at https://www.igi-global.com/publish/contributor-resources/before-you-write/ prior to submission. All submitted chapters will be reviewed on a double-anonymized review basis. Contributors may also be requested to serve as reviewers for this project. Note: There are no submission or acceptance fees for manuscripts submitted to this book publication, Theory and Practice in Horror Transmedia Fandom and Creation. All manuscripts are accepted based on a double-anonymized peer review editorial process. All proposals should be submitted through the eEditorial Discovery® online submission manager. Publisher This book is scheduled to be published by IGI Global Scientific Publishing, an international academic publisher of the "Information Science Reference", "Medical Information Science Reference", "Business Science Reference", and "Engineering Science Reference" imprints. IGI Global Scientific Publishing specializes in publishing reference books, scholarly journals, and electronic databases featuring academic research on a variety of innovative topic areas including, but not limited to, education, social science, medicine and healthcare, business and management, information science and technology, engineering, public administration, library and information science, media and communication studies, and environmental science. For additional information regarding the publisher, please visit https://www.igi-global.com. This publication is anticipated to be released in 2027. Indexing Information for Prospective Authors IGI Global Scientific Publishing meets the criteria for inclusion in major indexing services such as Scopus; however, it is important to note that all indexing decisions are made independently by these services. IGI Global Scientific Publishing books are selectively indexed by the indexing organization after publication. Indexing cannot be guaranteed for any book prior to publication, and the indexing organization has complete control over the final selection and timeline. Important Dates July 17, 2026: Proposal Submission Deadline July 31, 2026: Notification of Acceptance October 30, 2026: Full Chapter Submission January 1, 2027: Review Results Returned February 12, 2027: Final Acceptance Notification February 26, 2027: Final Chapter Submission Inquiries Jason DeHart University of Tennessee Knoxville dehartjason33@gmail.com Classifications Education; Library and Information Science; Media and Communications; Social Sciences and Humanities

items.fullDescription: Folklore is having a moment in South Asian writing, and it isn't a nostalgic one. Novelists, poets, memoirists, playwrights, and graphic novelists across the region and its diaspora keep returning to myth, oral narrative, legend, and vernacular ritual, not to decorate their work with the past, but to think through the pressures of the present: ecological collapse, historical trauma, gendered violence, migration, and a digital, algorithmic world the old tales never anticipated and somehow still speak to.

items.fullDescription: What is the real difference between speaking with nature and speaking for it? Is eco-centric thought a universally shared ideology, or does it develop in reaction to historical, philosophical, and socio-cultural contexts? In what way do the fundamental principles of Indian ecology vary from prevailing Western structures? These essential inquiries delineate the parameters of Ramachandra Guha’s Speaking with Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism (2024), which effectively contests the notion that environmentalism is a unidirectional phenomenon dictated by Western influence. This view posits that the rest of the world, particularly the Global South, lacks eco-conscious awareness because it is ‘too poor to be green’.

items.fullDescription: In India, the displacement of Adivasis, tribals, poor, farmers, forest-dwelling and land-based people, and other marginalized communities for development and infrastructure projects like dams, railways, power projects, and bridge construction, or for capitalist accumulation like mining, resource extraction, tourism, and industry, is a common occurrence. The trajectory of such displacement has a long history, starting in the colonial period and being aggravated in the postcolonial period under the Nehruvian model of development. Although such projects are implemented for the sake of the ‘greater common good’ for all, only a few elites enjoy the benefit of these projects, depriving millions of displaced, marginalized people (Roy 1999).

items.fullDescription: PCA True Crime CFP 2027 PCA/ACA will be held from March 24-27th, 2027 in Boston, MA The True Crime area co-chairs invite papers and presentations on all aspects of True Crime, including but not limited to analysis and interpretations across a range of media such as books, podcasts, film/documentaries, and television. Papers may deal with case narratives, psychology of a crime, media literacy, or investigative journalism. We recognize the interdisciplinarity of the True Crime genre, and also welcome submissions that explore topics such as gender/demographics of audiences, perpetrators or victims; media literacy of True Crime; sensationalizing high profile cases; criminology, victimology, and forensics; wrongful convictions and advocacy; prevention of crime, family/victim consent, and survivor stories; crimes against POC, indigenous groups, or marginalized peoples; and more. Presentations should be aware of and respectful to victims and their families as applicable to the specific topic being explored. Covering a vast expanse of time and an array of potential topics, True Crime offers countless opportunities for interdisciplinary academic study and debate. While opponents of the genre often critique crime stories as being exploitative and potentially traumatic for victims, society's perennial fascination with stories of crime, murder, and mayhem also provide insight into our collective interests, motivations, and prejudices. Significantly, the presentation of crime stories provides insight into our changing perspectives on criminality, deviant behavior, and the treatment of victims over time. In his Introduction to True Crime: An American Anthology, Harold Schechter writes: "What differs strikingly from era to era is the way such transgressions are interpreted. Acts otherwise analogous have been seen at different times as arising from sin, or irrational thinking, or mental disease, or inarticulate protest against abuse or oppression" (xix). In other words, the study of True Crime is also the study of our culture and its behaviors and beliefs. We look forward to presentations exploring our current moment of True Crime. Note: Due to the mentioned interdisciplinarity of True Crime, for the 2027 conference we are actively looking for submissions that would work as joint panels with other areas including Mystery & Detective Fiction or Vampire Studies. We encourage topics that explore the mutual influence and exchange between True Crime and crime fiction or the study of cases that involve influences from vampire-based lore. You may indicate in your proposal if you would like your paper to be considered for a joint panel; even if not accepted for a joint panel, your abstract will be considered for our regular True Crime programming. Submission Requirements: Proposals for single papers and panels should be up to 300 words and must include the following: 1) a title reflecting your argument (or framing concept in case of a panel or roundtable) 2) a clear statement of your argument/thesis and/or key research questions 3) an identification of the corpus that will be the focus of your study All paper proposals should be submitted directly through the PCA website. If you are organizing a panel of 3-4 speakers, or a roundtable discussion panel of 4-6 participants, please have your panelists submit proposals directly to the PCA website and contact the True Crime co-chairs with a panel proposal identifying your presenters. Otherwise, proposals will be arranged into panel sessions based on critical, disciplinary, or thematic connectivity. Co-chairs for True Crime: Dr. Lauren Kuryloski, (lkurylos@buffalo.edu) and Dr. Samantha Przybylowicz Axtell, (samantha.przybylowicz@gmail.com).

items.title: Irony: Dramatic and Otherwise
items.location: University of Tübingen, Germany · Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate
items.excerpt: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it e...
items.fullDescription: Literary irony is a phenomenon that seems expressly invented for the approach Connotations: A Journal for Critical Debate (www.connotations.de) wishes to promote, namely combining the close reading of literary texts with wider theoretical perspectives. Clearly, irony is a textual feature, and it equally clearly reaches beyond individual texts in that it evokes and reflects basic constituents of human communication: in particular, the relationship between what is said and what is meant and the relationship between what is said and what is known. Irony comes into play when these relationships are marked by significant discrepancies. The discrepancy between what is said and what is meant is essential for verbal irony and the discrepancy between what is said and what is known is fundamental to dramatic (or narrative) irony. If and how these two kinds of irony belong together, however, is a moot point and one of the questions to be addressed by our symposium. Thus the unequal distribution of knowledge (between characters and/or between characters and the reader) which marks narrative and dramatic irony may be related to the divergence which characterizes verbal irony. When Viola in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, disguised as a boy, says to Orsino: "I am all the daughters of my father's house," Orsino, who believes Viola to be a young man, must regard this statement as verbal irony on Viola's part. What is said ("daughters") is very different from what appears to be meant ("sons"). To us, the audience, however, this is a case of dramatic irony since we know that Viola is a woman and we observe Orsino's ignorance. What makes this case particularly intriguing is that here dramatic irony is not based on a discrepancy between what is said and what we know since Viola literally speaks the truth. The discrepancy arises between what we know and what is supposed to be spoken ironically. The example shows that asking about the relationship between verbal and dramatic/narrative irony entails numerous other questions that the Connotations symposium is going to address. In particular, we will ask about effects of irony, both with regard to characters and the audience. What is the added value of an ironic remark? What does it tell us about the speaker? In what way does an ironic utterance signal that there is a common ground between the communication partners? Are the inclusion and exclusion of others, i.e. those who get the ironical meaning and those who don't, similar to cases of discrepant awareness? How do we know that an utterance is meant ironically and how are we to deal with ambiguity in this respect? Can non-verbal irony markers be encoded in literary texts? Are theories of verbal irony based on notions of echo and pretence relatable to drama and fiction? We invite papers focussing on these and related questions, based on literature in English from the Middle Ages to the present. Please send an abstract (300 words max.) to the editors of Connotations at symposium2027@connotations.de by 31 October 2026

items.fullDescription: Call for Papers SPORTS AND POPULAR CULTURE Southwest Popular / American Culture Association (SWPACA) 48th Annual Conference, February 17-20, 2027 Marriott Albuquerque Albuquerque, New Mexico https://swpaca.org/ Submissions open: September 1, 2026 Proposal submission deadline: October 31, 2026 Proposals for papers and panels are now being accepted for the 48th annual SWPACA conference. One of the nation's largest interdisciplinary academic conferences, SWPACA offers nearly 70 subject areas, each typically featuring multiple panels. For a full list of subject areas, area descriptions, and Area Chairs, please visit https://swpaca.org/subject-areas/. The chair for the Sports and Popular Culture area welcomes proposals from interested scholars for the upcoming Southwest Popular/American Culture Association virtual conference. We invite proposals pertaining to any aspect of the intersection of sports and popular culture, including (but not limited to): Scandals (Lance Armstrong, Black Sox, Houston Astros) Films on a particular sport (Field of Dreams, Million Dollar Baby, The Blind Side) Separate but also unequal: pay disparities between female and male athletes Female boxers in popular culture Sports in anime "Friday Night Lights" and football culture in Texas Sports memorabilia in popular culture NIL policies in sports today Doping scandals and their effect on the fans Legal cases and their effect on sports Fandom and sports Sports in literature Young adult sports fiction All proposals must be submitted through the conference's database at https://swpaca.org/app. For details on using the submission database and on the application process in general (including submitting proposals for roundtables and preformed panels), please see the FAQS & Resources tab on https://swpaca.org/. Individual proposals for 15-minute papers must include an abstract of approximately 200-500 words and a brief summary of 100 words or less. For information on how to submit a proposal for a multi-paper panel, please view the above FAQs & Resources link. The deadline for submissions is October 31, 2026. SWPACA offers monetary awards for the best graduate student papers in a variety of categories. Submissions of accepted, full papers are due January 1, 2027. More details are here: https://swpaca.org/graduate-student-paper-awards/. SWPACA also offers travel fellowships for undergraduate and graduate students as well as contingent faculty: https://swpaca.org/travel-awards-students-faculty/. Registration and travel information for the conference is available at https://swpaca.org/albuquerque-conference/. In addition, please check out the organization's peer-reviewed, scholarly journal, Dialogue: The Interdisciplinary Journal of Popular Culture and Pedagogy, at https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/dialogue/. If you have any questions about the Sports and Popular Culture area, please contact its Area Chair, Stacy Fowler, St. Mary's University, at sfowler@stmarytx.edu. If you have general questions about the conference, please contact us at support@swpaca.org, and a member of the executive team will get back to you. This will be a fully in-person conference. If you're looking for an online option to present your work, keep an eye out for details about the 2027 SWPACA Summer Salon, a completely virtual conference to take place in June 2027. We look forward to receiving your submissions!
